entries.1:1: Ezekiel was a prisoner far from home when God opened the heavens and gave him a vision. It means God can speak to people even in hard, hopeless places.
entries.1:2: This gives the exact date of the vision, counting from when King Jehoiachin was taken captive. It shows the vision happened at a real, specific time in history.
entries.1:3: God's message came personally to Ezekiel, a priest living among exiles in Babylon, and God's power was with him there. It means God's presence and word reach people even in a foreign land.
entries.1:4: Ezekiel saw a huge storm coming from the north with fire and bright light, and something glowing like polished metal in the middle. It sets the scene for a powerful, awe-inspiring encounter with God.
entries.1:5: Inside the fire were four strange living creatures that looked partly human. These are heavenly beings that serve God.
entries.1:6: Each creature had four faces and four wings. The strange details show these are not ordinary creatures but something from God's heavenly realm.
entries.1:7: Their legs were straight and their feet gleamed like polished bronze. The shining metal suggests strength and glory.
entries.1:8: They had human hands under their wings, and faces on all four sides. This mixing of human and heavenly features shows they are close to God and ready to act.
entries.1:9: They moved straight ahead without turning. It means they go exactly where they are meant to go, without hesitation.
entries.1:10: Each creature had a human face, a lion's face, an ox's face, and an eagle's face. These likely picture strength, service, and swiftness under God's command.
entries.1:11: Their wings were spread out and also covered their bodies. The wings show readiness to move and reverence before God.
entries.1:12: They went wherever the spirit wanted them to go, straight ahead without turning. It means they were completely guided by God's Spirit.
entries.1:13: Between the creatures was something like burning coals and flashing fire, with lightning coming out. It shows God's presence is powerful and holy.
entries.1:14: The creatures darted back and forth as fast as lightning. It shows they move with great speed and energy.
entries.1:15: Beside each of the four creatures Ezekiel saw a wheel on the ground. The wheels are part of this heavenly scene.
entries.1:16: The wheels sparkled like a precious stone, and each looked like a wheel inside another wheel. This suggests they can move in any direction.
entries.1:17: The wheels could go straight in any of four directions without turning aside. It means movement is free and unhindered.
entries.1:18: The rims of the wheels were covered with eyes all around. The eyes suggest full awareness and watchfulness.
entries.1:19: When the creatures moved, the wheels moved with them, and when they rose up, the wheels rose too. Everything moves together in perfect coordination.
entries.1:20: The creatures went wherever the spirit wanted, and the wheels rose with them because the same spirit was in the wheels. It shows everything is driven by one guiding Spirit.
entries.1:21: The wheels and creatures moved and stopped together because the spirit of the creatures was in the wheels. It means the whole scene moves as one under God's direction.
entries.1:22: Above the creatures was something like a clear, icy dome stretched out over their heads. It looks like a platform separating earth from God's throne above.
entries.1:23: Under the dome their wings were spread out straight, with two wings covering each body. The wings show both readiness and humility.
entries.1:24: When they moved, their wings sounded like rushing water, like God's own voice, like a mighty army; when they stopped, they lowered their wings. The sound shows God's power and majesty.
entries.1:25: A voice came from above the dome over their heads, and when they stopped they lowered their wings. It shows someone above is speaking and the creatures respond in reverence.
entries.1:26: Above the dome was something like a throne of sapphire, and on it was a figure like a man. This is a picture of God's throne and his glorious presence.
entries.1:27: The figure glowed like polished metal with fire above and below, surrounded by bright light. It shows God's glory is overwhelming and beyond full description.
entries.1:28: The surrounding light looked like a rainbow on a rainy day, and this was the glory of the Lord; Ezekiel fell face down and heard a voice speaking. It means God's glory is beautiful and awe-inspiring, and the right response is humble worship.
entries.2:1: God tells Ezekiel to stand up so he can hear what God is about to say. It means God wants us ready and paying attention when he speaks to us.
entries.2:2: As soon as God spoke, his Spirit entered Ezekiel and lifted him to his feet, and he heard God's voice. It shows God's Spirit gives us the strength to do what he asks.
entries.2:3: God is sending Ezekiel to the people of Israel, who have rebelled against God and kept sinning for generations. It means God still reaches out to people who have turned away from him.
entries.2:4: The people are stubborn and hard-hearted, but Ezekiel must still deliver God's message to them. It means we should speak God's truth even when people are unlikely to listen.
entries.2:5: Whether the people listen or not, they will know a prophet has been among them. It means our job is to be faithful in sharing God's message, and the results are up to God.
entries.2:6: God tells Ezekiel not to be afraid of these people or their harsh words, even though living among them is like being surrounded by thorns and scorpions. It means God's presence gives us courage when people are hostile to his message.
entries.2:7: Ezekiel must speak God's words to the people regardless of whether they listen, because they are rebellious. It means we should not let people's rejection stop us from doing what God has called us to do.
entries.2:8: God warns Ezekiel not to be rebellious like the people, but to open his mouth and receive what God gives him. It means we should stay humble and obedient, ready to take in God's words.
entries.2:9: Ezekiel sees a hand reaching out to him holding a scroll. It means God himself is providing the message Ezekiel is to deliver.
entries.2:10: The scroll is unrolled before Ezekiel, and it is covered front and back with words of grief, sorrow, and trouble. It means the message God gives is a heavy one of coming judgment, not easy or pleasant news.
entries.3:1: God tells Ezekiel to take in his message completely, as if eating it, and then go deliver it to the people of Israel. It means the messenger must first absorb God's word before speaking it to others.
entries.3:2: Ezekiel obeyed and received God's message as something to take inside himself. It shows that hearing from God is meant to become part of who you are, not just words you hear.
entries.3:3: God tells Ezekiel to fill himself with the scroll, and when he does, it tastes sweet like honey. God's message may be hard, but receiving it is good and satisfying.
entries.3:4: God sends Ezekiel to the people of Israel to speak God's words to them. The task is simple and direct: go and say what God gives you to say.
entries.3:5: Ezekiel is not being sent to foreigners with a strange language but to his own people. That makes the job harder, because those closest to him should understand but may not listen.
entries.3:6: God says that foreign peoples would actually listen more readily than Israel will. Sometimes those far off are more open to God than those who grew up with him.
entries.3:7: Israel will refuse to listen because they have set themselves against God. Their stubbornness is really toward God, not just toward the prophet.
entries.3:8: God makes Ezekiel as stubborn and strong as the people he faces. God gives him the toughness he needs to stand before a hard-hearted audience.
entries.3:9: God makes Ezekiel's resolve as hard as diamond so he won't be intimidated by their faces. God promises courage to face people who resist his message.
entries.3:10: God tells Ezekiel to take his words deeply to heart and listen carefully. Before you speak for God, you must first truly hear him.
entries.3:11: Ezekiel is to go to his fellow exiles and tell them what God says, whether they listen or not. The messenger's job is to speak faithfully; the response is up to the hearers.
entries.3:12: The Spirit lifts Ezekiel up, and he hears a loud sound as God's glory moves from its place. It shows God's presence is powerful and active, not distant.
entries.3:13: Ezekiel hears the wings of the living creatures and the wheels beside them, a loud rushing sound. This describes the impressive, moving presence of God that he witnessed.
entries.3:14: The Spirit carries Ezekiel away, and he goes with strong inner emotion while God's hand rests powerfully on him. Serving God can involve deep feeling and a sense of being carried along by him.
entries.3:15: Ezekiel arrives among the exiles at Tel-abib by the Chebar River and sits with them stunned for seven days. Even a prophet needs time to absorb a heavy calling before speaking.
entries.3:16: After seven days, God speaks to Ezekiel again. God's timing matters; he gives his messenger time before the next instruction.
entries.3:17: God appoints Ezekiel as a watchman who must warn Israel of coming danger. A watchman's job is to pass on God's warning clearly, not to stay silent.
entries.3:18: If Ezekiel fails to warn a wicked person, that person dies for his sin, but God holds Ezekiel responsible for not speaking. We are accountable for whether we warn people of danger we know about.
entries.3:19: If Ezekiel warns the wicked person and he still refuses to change, he dies for his sin, but Ezekiel is not to blame. Faithful warning is what matters, even when the response is rejection.
entries.3:20: If a good person turns to evil and Ezekiel doesn't warn him, that person dies and his past good deeds are forgotten, and Ezekiel is held responsible. Past goodness doesn't excuse present sin, and the messenger must still warn.
entries.3:21: If Ezekiel warns the good person not to sin and he listens, he lives and Ezekiel is safe. A faithful warning can save a life and clears the messenger of blame.
entries.3:22: God's hand is on Ezekiel, and God tells him to go out into the valley to meet with him. God sometimes calls people away to a quiet place for a personal encounter.
entries.3:23: Ezekiel goes to the valley and sees God's glory there, just as he had by the river, and he falls face down. God's glory is overwhelming and calls for humble reverence.
entries.3:24: The Spirit enters Ezekiel and sets him on his feet, then tells him to shut himself inside his house. God strengthens him for obedience, even when that obedience means isolation.
entries.3:25: God says Ezekiel will be bound with cords so he cannot go out among the people. God may restrict a messenger's movements as part of his plan.
entries.3:26: God will make Ezekiel's tongue stick to the roof of his mouth so he cannot speak or argue with the people. Sometimes God silences his messenger until the right time.
entries.3:27: When God speaks to Ezekiel, he will open his mouth, and Ezekiel must deliver God's message; those who will listen may listen, and those who won't may refuse. The messenger speaks God's word and leaves the response to the hearers.
entries.4:1: God tells Ezekiel to draw a picture of Jerusalem on a brick as a visual message. It shows the reader that God sometimes uses everyday objects to make His warnings clear.
entries.4:2: Ezekiel is to act out an army attacking the city, building siege works and battering rams around it. This pictures the real siege that was coming on Jerusalem because of the people's sin.
entries.4:3: An iron pan set between Ezekiel and the city shows that God is against Jerusalem and will not hear its cries. It warns the reader that stubborn sin can shut a person off from God.
entries.4:4: Ezekiel lies on his left side to carry the guilt of Israel's sin in a symbolic way. It shows how seriously God takes sin and how long its consequences can last.
entries.4:5: The 390 days stand for the years of Israel's sin that Ezekiel must bear in this sign. It reminds the reader that God counts sin carefully and does not overlook it.
entries.4:6: After that, Ezekiel lies on his right side for 40 days, one day for each year of Judah's sin. It shows that judgment comes on both kingdoms and that God's timing is exact.
entries.4:7: Ezekiel faces the besieged city with his arm bared, like a prophet announcing its doom. It means God's message against Jerusalem was certain and would surely happen.
entries.4:8: God ties Ezekiel up so he cannot turn over until the sign is finished. It shows that the prophet is completely under God's control and that the judgment cannot be escaped.
entries.4:9: Ezekiel must mix several grains into one bread and eat it during the whole sign. It pictures the scarce and poor food people would eat during a siege.
entries.4:10: He may eat only a small weighed amount of food each day. It shows the reader how hunger and rationing would come on the people under judgment.
entries.4:11: He may drink only a small measured amount of water each day. It pictures the thirst and fear that would come when a city is cut off.
entries.4:12: Ezekiel is told to bake his bread over human waste in front of the people. It is a disgusting sign of how unclean and humiliating life would become in exile.
entries.4:13: God explains that Israel will eat ritually unclean food among the nations where He scatters them. It means exile would strip away their clean way of life and humble them.
entries.4:14: Ezekiel protests that he has never eaten unclean or defiled food in his whole life. It shows his sincere desire to obey God and his shock at this command.
entries.4:15: God graciously lets him use cow dung instead of human waste to bake the bread. It shows that God listens to His servant and shows mercy even in judgment.
entries.4:16: God says He will cut off Jerusalem's supply of bread and water so people weigh and ration them in fear. It means the basic needs of life would become scarce because of sin.
entries.4:17: People will lack bread and water, stare at each other in shock, and waste away in their sin. It shows that sin leads to ruin and that God's warning is meant to turn people back to Him.
entries.5:1: God tells Ezekiel to act out a picture using a sharp sword as a razor and scales to weigh the cut hair. It is a visual sign of coming judgment on Jerusalem, showing that God's warning is serious and deliberate.
entries.5:2: The hair is divided into three parts to show three fates: some burned inside the city, some struck by the sword outside, and some scattered to the wind with a sword chasing them. It means the people will face destruction in several ways, and none will escape easily.
entries.5:3: Ezekiel keeps a few hairs tucked in his clothing, showing that a small remnant will be preserved. It means not everyone will be destroyed; God keeps a few safe.
entries.5:4: Some of the saved hairs are thrown into the fire, showing that even among the survivors trouble will continue. It means being spared does not mean life will be easy, and God's warning applies even to the remnant.
entries.5:5: God identifies Jerusalem as the city at the center of the nations. It means Jerusalem had a special place and responsibility before God, so its failure matters more.
entries.5:6: Jerusalem rebelled against God's commands and behaved worse than the nations around her. It means knowing God's rules and ignoring them is serious, and rebellion is measured against what was known.
entries.5:7: Because Jerusalem was more unruly than the surrounding nations and followed their customs instead of God's rules, God announces judgment. It means copying the world's ways instead of God's leads to trouble.
entries.5:8: God says plainly that he is against his people and will judge them openly before other nations. It means God does not ignore sin in his own people, and the consequences will be seen by everyone.
entries.5:9: God will bring a judgment so severe it has no parallel, because of the people's disgusting practices. It means sin has real and terrible consequences, and God takes it seriously.
entries.5:10: The judgment will be so harsh that family members turn on each other, and the survivors will be scattered. It means sin breaks families and communities apart, and God's warning is meant to be heard.
entries.5:11: Because the people defiled God's holy place with their hated and disgusting practices, God will withdraw mercy and pity. It means treating what God calls holy with contempt has serious results.
entries.5:12: The people will be divided into three groups facing disease, sword, and scattering, with a sword pursuing even the scattered. It means judgment will reach everyone, and running away will not bring safety.
entries.5:13: God's anger will run its full course and then rest, and the people will know that he has spoken. It means God's judgment is not random but purposeful, and it will make clear who he is.
entries.5:14: Jerusalem will become a ruin and an object of shame among the surrounding nations. It means the city that was meant to honor God will become a warning to others.
entries.5:15: The city will become a shame, a bitter saying, and a shocking example to the nations when God carries out his judgment. It means God's people's failure becomes a public lesson about the cost of rebellion.
entries.5:16: God will send deadly disease like arrows and cut off the food supply. It means the judgment includes both sickness and hunger, and God is the one behind it.
entries.5:17: God will send famine, wild animals, disease, violent death, and the sword against the people. It means the warnings are comprehensive and certain, and God himself has declared it.
entries.6:1: God is speaking directly to the prophet Ezekiel, giving him a message to deliver. It reminds the reader that what follows is not Ezekiel's own opinion but words that came from God.
entries.6:2: God tells Ezekiel to face the mountains of Israel and speak a prophecy to them. The reader sees that God uses a person to announce his message, even to the land itself.
entries.6:3: God announces that he is bringing war and destruction on the hills, valleys, and streams of Israel, targeting the places where people worshiped other gods. It means judgment is coming on the centers of false worship, not just on individuals.
entries.6:4: The altars and idols will be smashed, and dead bodies will be laid in front of them. It shows that the false gods people trusted cannot protect them or themselves.
entries.6:5: The bodies and bones of Israelites will be scattered around their idols and altars. This pictures total humiliation for a people who had turned to idols instead of God.
entries.6:6: Everywhere people live, towns will be ruined and worship sites destroyed until the idols and images are wiped out. It means the whole system of false worship will be brought to nothing.
entries.6:7: People will die throughout the land, and the survivors will finally recognize that God is the Lord. It means judgment will make God's reality unmistakable.
entries.6:8: Even in judgment, God will spare a small number and scatter them among other nations. It shows that God does not completely abandon his people; a remnant survives.
entries.6:9: The survivors will remember God in exile and grieve over how their unfaithful hearts and eyes led them to idols. It means they will feel real sorrow for their sin and turn back to God.
entries.6:10: They will know that God is the Lord and that his warnings were not empty threats. It means God's words can be trusted, even when they are hard.
entries.6:11: God tells Ezekiel to clap and stamp in grief over the coming disaster of war, famine, and disease. It means the prophet shares God's sorrow over sin and its consequences.
entries.6:12: No one will escape: those far off will die of disease, those nearby by the sword, and those trapped by famine. It means judgment will reach everyone, showing how seriously God takes their sin.
entries.6:13: Dead bodies will lie around the idols and altars on every hill and under every tree where people burned offerings to false gods. It means the places of idol worship will become places of death, proving the idols are powerless.
entries.6:14: God will stretch out his hand and make the land empty and desolate from one end to the other. It means the whole land will feel the consequences of turning away from God, and people will know he is the Lord.
entries.7:1: God is speaking directly to Ezekiel, giving him a message to pass on. It reminds the reader that what follows is presented as God's own words, not Ezekiel's opinion.
entries.7:2: God tells Ezekiel to announce that Israel's time is up and disaster is coming on the whole land. The reader is meant to feel the seriousness of a warning that leaves no area untouched.
entries.7:3: God says the judgment has arrived and he will hold the people responsible for how they have lived and for their shameful deeds. It means wrongdoing does not go unnoticed forever.
entries.7:4: God says he will not hold back pity but will let the consequences of the people's own actions fall on them. The reader learns that God's patience has limits and that actions carry real results.
entries.7:5: God announces that a specific disaster is on its way. The repetition stresses that this is certain, not just a possibility.
entries.7:6: The same warning is repeated: the end is coming and it is near. It presses the reader to take the warning seriously rather than put it off.
entries.7:7: The day of reckoning has arrived for the people of the land and will not be delayed. It means the moment of accountability cannot be postponed or avoided.
entries.7:8: God says he will soon pour out his anger and judge the people for their ways and shameful acts. The reader sees that God responds to persistent wrongdoing with real consequences.
entries.7:9: Again God says he will show no pity but will repay people for their own conduct. The purpose is that they will finally recognize who God is.
entries.7:10: The day of judgment has arrived, and the people's corruption and pride are now showing openly like a plant in bloom. It means hidden bad character eventually becomes visible.
entries.7:11: Violence has grown into a weapon of evil, and it will not be delayed. The reader sees that unchecked violence eventually turns destructive.
entries.7:12: The time is so near that buyers and sellers should not bother celebrating or grieving over deals. It means ordinary business plans matter little when judgment is at the door.
entries.7:13: A trader will never get back what he sold, even if he lives on. It means the normal cycles of buying and selling are being cut off by coming disaster.
entries.7:14: The buyer will never receive what he paid for, because God's anger is on everyone. It shows that no one will escape the consequences.
entries.7:15: Danger waits outside the city and disease and hunger wait inside it, so there is no safe place. The reader sees that judgment reaches every situation.
entries.7:16: Those who manage to escape will hide away and still die, each one because of his own sin. It means running away does not solve the problem of guilt.
entries.7:17: Everyone's hands will go limp and their knees will give way like water. It pictures total helplessness and fear when judgment comes.
entries.7:18: People will wear rough mourning clothes, be gripped by terror, and feel deep shame. It shows how completely disaster will humble them.
entries.7:19: People will throw their silver and gold into the streets because money cannot save them on the day of God's anger; their wealth became the very thing that led them into sin. It warns the reader that riches are useless when it comes to standing before God.
entries.7:20: The people took the beautiful things God gave them and used them to make idols, so God now treats those things as unclean. It means good gifts can be ruined when they are turned into objects of worship.
entries.7:21: God will hand the city's treasures over to foreigners and wicked people who will take them and defile them. It shows that what people trusted in for security can be stripped away.
entries.7:22: God will turn away from his people and let violent outsiders enter and defile his sacred place. It means his protective presence is withdrawn because of their sin.
entries.7:23: God commands that a chain be made, symbolizing captivity, because the land is full of bloodshed and violence. The reader sees that a society full of cruelty brings its own downfall.
entries.7:24: God will bring the most ruthless nations to take over the people's homes and end their proud strength, and their holy places will be defiled. It means no human strength or religion can shield a people who have abandoned God.
entries.7:25: Terror is coming, and people will search desperately for peace but find none. It shows that peace cannot be manufactured once judgment has begun.
entries.7:26: Disaster will pile on disaster, and the guidance people relied on—prophets, priests, and elders—will fail them. It means when a society rejects God, even its trusted leaders lose wisdom.
entries.7:27: The king will mourn, the ruler will be stunned, and ordinary people will be paralyzed with fear, because God will judge them fairly for how they have lived. The outcome is that everyone will know God is the Lord.
entries.8:1: Ezekiel was sitting at home with the leaders of Judah when he suddenly felt God's power come over him. It shows that God can reach people right where they are, in ordinary moments.
entries.8:2: Ezekiel saw a figure that looked like a man made of fire and glowing metal. This was a heavenly being showing God's glory and power.
entries.8:3: The figure lifted Ezekiel by the hair and carried him in a vision to Jerusalem, to a place where an idol stood. God was showing Ezekiel what was really happening in the temple.
entries.8:4: Ezekiel saw God's glory there, just as he had seen it before in the valley. God was still present even in a place full of wrong worship.
entries.8:5: God told Ezekiel to look north, and he saw an idol standing near the altar entrance. This idol was making God jealous because his people were worshiping it.
entries.8:6: God asked Ezekiel if he saw the disgusting things Israel was doing, things that drove God away from his own temple. He warned that even worse things were coming.
entries.8:7: God brought Ezekiel to a doorway and showed him a hole in the wall. This was the start of revealing hidden sins.
entries.8:8: God told Ezekiel to dig through the wall, and when he did, he found a hidden door. It shows that secret sins can be uncovered.
entries.8:9: God told Ezekiel to go inside and see the evil things the people were doing in secret. God sees what people try to hide.
entries.8:10: Inside, Ezekiel saw the walls covered with pictures of crawling creatures, unclean animals, and idols. The leaders were surrounding themselves with images of false gods.
entries.8:11: Seventy leaders of Israel were standing there burning incense to these idols, with Jaazaniah leading them. The leaders themselves were deep in idol worship.
entries.8:12: God told Ezekiel that these leaders did this in the dark, thinking God couldn't see them and had left the land. They were fooling themselves, because God sees everything.
entries.8:13: God told Ezekiel he would see even worse things than this. The sin was getting deeper and more serious.
entries.8:14: Ezekiel was shown women at the temple gate crying for Tammuz, a false god. God's people were mixing pagan mourning rituals with worship of him.
entries.8:15: God asked Ezekiel if he had seen this, and said even worse things were still to come. The corruption was not yet at its worst.
entries.8:16: About twenty-five men stood in the temple courtyard with their backs to God's temple, facing east and worshiping the sun. They had literally turned their backs on God.
entries.8:17: God asked if these disgusting things were a small matter, since the people also filled the land with violence and insulted God. Their sins were piling up and making God angry.
entries.8:18: Because of all this, God said he would pour out his anger without mercy or pity. This is a serious warning that sin has real consequences.
entries.9:1: God calls for the city's guards to come forward with their weapons, ready to act. It shows that judgment is about to begin and is under God's command.
entries.9:2: Six armed men and a man in linen carrying writing tools arrive and stand by the altar. This sets the scene for both judgment and the marking of those who will be spared.
entries.9:3: God's glory moves from above the cherubim to the temple doorway, showing he is leaving his dwelling place. He then speaks to the man with the inkpot.
entries.9:4: God tells the man to mark the foreheads of people who grieve over the city's sins. Those who are troubled by evil are marked and protected.
entries.9:5: God orders the armed men to follow and kill without showing mercy. The judgment is severe and comes directly from God's command.
entries.9:6: The killing includes old and young, but anyone with the mark is spared, and it begins at the temple. Judgment starts with God's own people and their leaders.
entries.9:7: The men are told to fill the temple courts and streets with the dead as they move through the city. The place that should have been holy becomes defiled by slaughter.
entries.9:8: Ezekiel falls face down and pleads with God not to destroy all of Israel. He shows compassion and intercedes even while the judgment is happening.
entries.9:9: God explains that the sin of Israel and Judah is enormous, with bloodshed and injustice everywhere. The people wrongly believe God has abandoned the land and cannot see what they do.
entries.9:10: God says he will not spare them but will bring their own conduct back on their heads. Sin has consequences, and God will not overlook it.
entries.9:11: The man in linen reports that he has completed the task of marking the people. The faithful few are secured before judgment falls.
entries.10:1: Ezekiel sees something like a throne made of sapphire above the strange winged creatures. This shows God is ruling in majesty even in a vision of judgment.
entries.10:2: God tells the man in linen to scoop burning coals from among the creatures and scatter them over the city. This pictures God's judgment being poured out on Jerusalem.
entries.10:3: The winged creatures stood at the right side of the temple while the man went in, and the courtyard was filled with a cloud. The cloud signals God's holy presence.
entries.10:4: God's glory rose from the creatures and settled over the temple doorway, filling the house with cloud and the courtyard with bright glory. God's presence is both awesome and overwhelming.
entries.10:5: The sound of the creatures' wings could be heard even in the outer courtyard, like the voice of God Almighty. This shows how powerful and unmistakable God's presence is.
entries.10:6: When God commanded the man in linen to take fire from between the wheels and creatures, the man went in and stood by a wheel. He obeyed exactly what God told him.
entries.10:7: The man reached into the fire among the creatures, took some, and went out. He carried out God's judgment as instructed.
entries.10:8: Ezekiel noticed what looked like human hands under the wings of the creatures. This strange detail shows these heavenly beings serve God with skill and purpose.
entries.10:9: Ezekiel saw four wheels beside the creatures, one by each, and they looked like sparkling beryl stone. The wheels show God's throne can move and act anywhere.
entries.10:10: All four wheels looked the same, like one wheel set inside another. This suggests they could move in any direction without difficulty.
entries.10:11: The wheels moved straight in whatever direction they faced without turning. They went wherever the leading one went, showing perfect coordination under God's direction.
entries.10:12: The rims of the wheels were covered with eyes all around. The eyes suggest full awareness and watchfulness.
entries.10:13: Ezekiel heard the wheels called "the circling wheels." The name highlights their constant, purposeful motion.
entries.10:14: Each creature had four faces: one like a winged being, one like a man, one like a lion, and one like an eagle. These faces picture strength, intelligence, and majesty in God's service.
entries.10:15: The creatures rose up, and Ezekiel recognized them as the same living beings he had seen by the river Chebar. This connects his earlier vision with what is happening now.
entries.10:16: Whenever the creatures moved, the wheels moved beside them, and when the creatures lifted their wings, the wheels stayed right with them. They move together as one.
entries.10:17: When the creatures stood still, the wheels stood still, and when they rose, the wheels rose too, because the spirit of life was in them. God's Spirit gives them life and unity.
entries.10:18: God's glory left the temple doorway and came to rest over the winged creatures. This signals that God's presence is departing from the temple.
entries.10:19: The creatures lifted their wings and rose with the wheels, stopping at the east gate of the Lord's house, with God's glory above them. God's glory is moving away from his house.
entries.10:20: Ezekiel confirms these were the same living beings he saw under the God of Israel by the river Chebar. He now understands clearly that they are the winged creatures.
entries.10:21: Each creature had four faces and four wings, with hands like human hands under their wings. These details match Ezekiel's earlier vision and show they are the same beings.
entries.10:22: Their faces looked the same as what Ezekiel saw by the river Chebar, and each one moved straight ahead. The vision is consistent, and their movement is direct and purposeful.
entries.11:1: God's Spirit brings Ezekiel to the temple's east gate, where he sees twenty-five leaders of the people, including two named rulers. This shows that the city's corruption reached even its top officials.
entries.11:2: God tells Ezekiel that these men are the ones planning evil and leading the whole city astray. Leaders who misuse their influence are held responsible by God.
entries.11:3: These men are saying it's not yet time to build houses, and they claim the city is a safe cooking pot and they are the meat kept safe inside. They are falsely confident that nothing bad will happen to them.
entries.11:4: God commands Ezekiel to speak prophetically against these men. God's word must be delivered even when it is directed at powerful people.
entries.11:5: The Spirit of the Lord comes on Ezekiel and tells him to declare God's message, saying that God knows exactly what the people have been thinking. Nothing in our minds is hidden from God.
entries.11:6: God points out that the people have filled the city's streets with the dead through violence and injustice. Their own actions have brought death into their midst.
entries.11:7: God turns their cooking-pot saying against them: the dead in the streets are the meat, and God will drag the living out of the city. Their false sense of safety will be shattered.
entries.11:8: The people fear war, but God says the very sword they dread will come upon them. Running from a threat does not remove it when God himself is behind it.
entries.11:9: God will drive them out of the city and hand them over to foreigners, and he will execute judgment on them there. Escape from the city will not mean escape from God.
entries.11:10: They will die by the sword, and God will judge them within the land of Israel, and then they will know that he is the Lord. Judgment itself will prove who God is.
entries.11:11: The city will not be their safe pot, and they will not be the protected meat inside it; God will judge them at Israel's border. Their confidence in the city's protection is misplaced.
entries.11:12: They will know God because they ignored his rules and instead followed the customs of the surrounding nations. God's people are judged for adopting the ways of those around them instead of his.
entries.11:13: While Ezekiel is still speaking, Pelatiah dies, and Ezekiel falls face down and cries out, asking whether God will destroy all that remains of Israel. God's judgment moves the prophet to urgent prayer for mercy.
entries.11:14: God responds to Ezekiel's cry with a new word. God answers the prayers of those who intercede for others.
entries.11:15: The people still in Jerusalem look down on the exiles, Ezekiel's own relatives and countrymen, telling them to stay far from the Lord and claiming the land for themselves. Those who remained were wrongly treating the displaced as outsiders to God.
entries.11:16: God says that although he scattered his people among the nations, he himself has been a sanctuary for them in those foreign lands. Distance from home does not mean distance from God's presence.
entries.11:17: God promises to gather his scattered people back from the countries where they fled and to give them the land of Israel again. God's promises of restoration reach beyond present loss.
entries.11:18: When they return, they will remove all the detestable and disgusting idols from the land. Restoration includes cleaning out the things that dishonored God.
entries.11:19: God promises to give them a new heart and a new spirit, replacing their hard, stone-like heart with a soft, living one. Real change comes as a gift from God, not from our own effort.
entries.11:20: The purpose of the new heart is that they will follow God's rules and obey his commands, and then they will truly be his people and he will be their God. Obedience flows from the heart God gives.
entries.11:21: But those who keep chasing after their detestable idols will receive the punishment their own ways deserve. God does not force a new heart on those who stubbornly cling to evil.
entries.11:22: The winged creatures lift their wings with the wheels beside them, and the glory of Israel's God rises above them. God's presence is on the move, not tied to one place.
entries.11:23: The glory of the Lord leaves the city and comes to rest on the mountain east of Jerusalem. God's presence departing the temple signals that judgment is near.
entries.11:24: The Spirit lifts Ezekiel and carries him in a vision back to the exiles in Babylonia, and the vision ends. God's messages reach his people even far from their homeland.
entries.11:25: Ezekiel tells the exiles everything the Lord had shown him. Faithful reporting of God's word is part of the prophet's task.
entries.12:1: God spoke directly to Ezekiel to give him a message. This reminds the reader that God still speaks and gives direction to people.
entries.12:2: The people around Ezekiel had eyes and ears but refused to understand or listen to God. It warns the reader that stubbornness can keep us from seeing and hearing what God is saying.
entries.12:3: God told Ezekiel to pack up his belongings and move in front of everyone, as a visible picture of people being forced from their homes. It shows the reader that God sometimes uses actions, not just words, to get a message across.
entries.12:4: Ezekiel was to carry his things out during the day and leave in the evening like a captive being taken away. The reader learns that the coming exile would be real and painful, not just a warning.
entries.12:5: Ezekiel was told to dig through the wall and escape through the hole in front of the people. This pictured how the people would try to slip away secretly when disaster came.
entries.12:6: Ezekiel carried his belongings on his back in the dark with his face covered, acting out the shame and fear of fleeing. God made him a living sign so the people could not miss the warning.
entries.12:7: Ezekiel obeyed exactly and did everything God commanded, even though it looked strange. His obedience shows the reader that following God's instructions matters more than looking normal.
entries.12:8: The next morning God spoke to Ezekiel again. This shows that God's guidance can come step by step rather than all at once.
entries.12:9: The people asked Ezekiel what he was doing, which was the opening God wanted for the message. The reader sees that God can use our actions to spark questions that lead to truth.
entries.12:10: The acted-out warning was about the ruler in Jerusalem and all the people with him. It means their leaders and the whole nation would face the same judgment.
entries.12:11: Ezekiel told them plainly that he was a sign and that what he did would happen to them, including being taken away as prisoners. The reader learns that God's warnings are serious and will come true.
entries.12:12: The ruler would try to escape in the dark, carrying his belongings and covering his face so no one would recognize him. It shows that even leaders cannot hide from what God has announced.
entries.12:13: God would catch the ruler like a hunted animal and bring him to Babylon, but he would not see the land and would die there. This means escape would fail and God's judgment would reach him wherever he went.
entries.12:14: Everyone helping the ruler and all his troops would be scattered in every direction, with danger chasing them. The reader sees that no army or alliance can protect people from God's judgment.
entries.12:15: When the people were scattered among other nations, they would finally recognize that God is the Lord. Even in punishment, God's purpose is to make himself known.
entries.12:16: God would spare a small number from war, hunger, and disease so they could admit their wrong ways among the nations. This shows that God's mercy leaves room for confession and change, even after failure.
entries.12:17: God spoke to Ezekiel again with another message. The reader is reminded that God keeps communicating and does not abandon his people without warning.
entries.12:18: Ezekiel was told to eat and drink while trembling with fear and worry. This acted out the anxiety and insecurity the people would feel when their world fell apart.
entries.12:19: The people of Jerusalem and Israel would eat and drink in fear because their land's wealth would be stripped away due to their violence. It teaches the reader that injustice and violence eventually bring ruin on a whole society.
entries.12:20: The populated towns would be left empty and the land would become a desolate sight, and then the people would know God is the Lord. It means that when everything is gone, people finally see who God is.
entries.12:21: God spoke to Ezekiel once more. This shows that God keeps addressing the excuses people make rather than letting them go unchallenged.
entries.12:22: People were saying that visions never come true and that time keeps passing with nothing happening. The reader learns how easy it is to dismiss God's warnings when they seem delayed.
entries.12:23: God said that saying would stop, because the days were near and every vision would actually happen. It means God's promises and warnings are not empty talk; they will come true.
entries.12:24: There would be no more false visions or misleading fortune-telling among Israel. God was promising that his true message would replace the lies people had been trusting.
entries.12:25: God declared that he would speak and then do it, without delay, even in the people's own lifetime. The reader can trust that what God says will happen, even if it seems slow.
entries.12:26: God gave Ezekiel yet another message. This repetition shows how patient God is in warning people again and again.
entries.12:27: The people were saying that Ezekiel's visions were for a distant future and did not matter now. It shows how people push God's warnings far away so they do not have to change.
entries.12:28: God answered that none of his words would be delayed any longer, and what he said he would do. The reader learns that God's timing is certain, and his words will not be put off forever.
entries.13:1: God spoke directly to Ezekiel, giving him a message to deliver. It reminds the reader that God still speaks and uses people to pass on what he says.
entries.13:2: God tells Ezekiel to speak against the prophets of Israel who were making up their own messages instead of hearing from God. It means we should check whether a message really comes from God or just from someone's imagination.
entries.13:3: God pronounces trouble on prophets who are foolish, following their own inner impulses rather than seeing anything from God. It warns the reader not to trust leaders who claim divine insight but have none.
entries.13:4: Israel's prophets are compared to jackals, scavengers that roam ruined places and do nothing to help. It means these leaders were useless when the people most needed real guidance.
entries.13:5: The prophets failed to stand in the gaps and repair the wall, meaning they did nothing to protect or strengthen the people for the coming day of trouble. It challenges the reader to notice leaders who avoid the hard work of guarding others.
entries.13:6: These prophets claimed visions and used divination, saying "the Lord says" when God had not sent them, hoping their words would come true anyway. It shows how empty claims can sound convincing but still be false.
entries.13:7: God confronts them directly: their visions were empty and their divination false, yet they spoke as if God had said it. It means claiming God's authority for your own words is a serious matter.
entries.13:8: Because their words were empty and their visions false, God says he is against them. It reminds the reader that God opposes those who misrepresent him.
entries.13:9: God will act against these false prophets: they will be cut off from his people's counsel, left out of Israel's records, and kept from the land. It means false teachers lose their place among God's people, and God's judgment will be evident.
entries.13:10: These prophets misled God's people by promising peace when there was none, and they covered over a flimsy wall with whitewash to make it look solid. It warns against leaders who make things look fine when the underlying situation is unsafe.
entries.13:11: God tells the whitewashers that a heavy storm, hail, and wind will come and split the wall apart. It means a false sense of security will not survive real trouble.
entries.13:12: When the wall collapses, people will ask where the whitewash went. It shows that the cover-up is exposed once the underlying weakness gives way.
entries.13:13: God himself will send the storm, the flooding rain, and the hail in his anger. It means the judgment is not random disaster but God's deliberate response to the deception.
entries.13:14: God will tear down the whitewashed wall to its foundation, and those who covered it will be destroyed with it. It means the false security and its makers fall together, and people will know God was behind it.
entries.13:15: God will pour out his anger on the wall and on those who whitewashed it, then ask where they all are. It means the deception and the deceivers will both be gone, exposed as nothing.
entries.13:16: These are the prophets who told Jerusalem everything would be peaceful when it wasn't. It means promising peace that God has not promised is a false message.
entries.13:17: God now turns Ezekiel against the women of his people who were acting as prophets on their own initiative. It shows that false spiritual leadership was not limited to men, and God opposed it too.
entries.13:18: God pronounces trouble on women who used magic bands and veils to trap people's lives, treating human souls as something to hunt and control. It warns against spiritual practices that manipulate people for personal gain.
entries.13:19: They disgraced God among his people for small payments, putting to death people who should live and keeping alive people who should not, by lying to those who listened. It means using religion for money and telling people what they want to hear does real harm.
entries.13:20: God is against the magic bands these women used to trap people, and he will tear them off and set the trapped people free. It means God himself rescues those caught by manipulative spiritual control.
entries.13:21: God will rip off their veils and free his people from their power so they can no longer be hunted. It means God breaks the grip of those who use religion to control others.
entries.13:22: Their lies discouraged honest people whom God had not grieved, and they encouraged evildoers to keep doing wrong instead of turning and living. It means false teaching damages the innocent and hardens the guilty.
entries.13:23: God ends their false visions and divination and frees his people from their control, so everyone will know he is the Lord. It means God shuts down deception and rescues those who were under it.
entries.14:1: Some of Israel's leaders came to Ezekiel and sat down in front of him, as if they wanted to hear from God. It shows that people can look religious on the outside while their hearts are somewhere else.
entries.14:2: God spoke to Ezekiel at that moment. This simply marks the start of God's message to the prophet.
entries.14:3: God says these men are still clinging to their idols in their hearts and holding on to the sin that ruins them. So it's a fair question whether God should give them guidance when they come asking.
entries.14:4: God tells Ezekiel to warn them: if anyone keeps idols in his heart and still comes to a prophet, God himself will answer that person in a way that matches his idols. You can't expect God to guide you while you're holding on to something you put before him.
entries.14:5: God's purpose is to win back the hearts of Israel, who have drifted away from him because of their idols. He acts to bring them back, not just to punish them.
entries.14:6: God calls Israel to turn back to him, to throw away their idols, and to stop looking to the things he finds detestable. Turning to God means actually letting go of what pulled you away.
entries.14:7: This applies to Israelites and to foreigners living among them alike: anyone who has turned from God yet still comes to a prophet for direction will get an answer from God himself. No one gets to keep idols and still expect friendly guidance.
entries.14:8: God will set his face against such a person, make him an example and a warning, and cut him off from his people. The result is that people will know God means what he says.
entries.14:9: If a prophet is deceived and gives a false message, God says he allowed that deception, and he will hold the prophet accountable and remove him from among his people. Teachers who mislead others are not off the hook.
entries.14:10: The prophet and the person who consulted him will share the same guilt and the same punishment. Both are responsible for going along with a lie.
entries.14:11: The goal is that Israel will stop wandering from God and stop defiling themselves with sin, so they can truly be his people and he their God. God's discipline aims at restoring the relationship.
entries.14:12: God spoke to Ezekiel again. This marks the beginning of a new message.
entries.14:13: If a country sins against God and he cuts off its food supply, that is his judgment on the land. Even basic survival becomes uncertain when a nation turns from him.
entries.14:14: Even if Noah, Daniel, and Job—famous for being righteous—were living there, their goodness would only save themselves, not the nation. You can't borrow someone else's righteousness to escape judgment.
entries.14:15: God describes another form of judgment: wild animals overrunning the land so that no one can travel through it. The land becomes desolate and dangerous.
entries.14:16: Even those three righteous men couldn't save their own children in that case—only themselves—and the land would still be ruined. Judgment on a nation is not cancelled by the presence of a few good people.
entries.14:17: God describes war as another judgment: a sword sweeping through the land, killing people and animals alike. Conflict becomes the instrument of his discipline.
entries.14:18: Again, even if those three men were there, they could save only themselves, not their sons or daughters. Personal righteousness has limits when a whole society is under judgment.
entries.14:19: God describes disease and bloodshed as yet another judgment, wiping out people and animals. Plague is pictured as his anger poured out on the land.
entries.14:20: Even Noah, Daniel, and Job together could only rescue themselves by their righteousness, not their children. Each person's standing before God is finally personal.
entries.14:21: If even those three couldn't stop judgment, how much less will Jerusalem escape when God sends all four punishments at once—war, famine, wild animals, and disease? The point is that no one should expect to be spared.
entries.14:22: Yet some survivors will remain, including sons and daughters, and they will come out to the exiles. When you see how they lived, you'll understand why judgment came and be comforted that it was justified.
entries.14:23: Seeing the survivors' ways will reassure you that God did not act without cause—everything he did had a reason. God's judgment is never arbitrary, even when it feels severe.
entries.15:1: God spoke directly to Ezekiel to give him a message. This reminds the reader that what follows is God's own word, not just a man's opinion.
entries.15:2: God asks Ezekiel to compare a vine to other trees in the forest. A vine is useful for fruit, but its wood is weak and worthless compared to trees that give good timber.
entries.15:3: God points out that vine wood is so useless you can't even make a simple peg from it to hang something on. It has no practical value as building material.
entries.15:4: Once vine wood is thrown in the fire, its ends burn and its middle chars, leaving it even more worthless. Burning it doesn't turn it into something useful.
entries.15:5: If vine wood was useless before it was burned, it is far more useless after being scorched. The point is that it has no purpose left at all.
entries.15:6: God says Jerusalem is like that useless vine wood, and he is handing the people over to be burned like fuel. Their special position did not protect them when they turned from him.
entries.15:7: God will set himself against them, and even those who escape one disaster will fall into another. When this happens, the people will finally recognize that God is the one acting.
entries.15:8: God will leave the land empty and ruined because of the people's evil. The reader is warned that persistent wrongdoing brings real judgment, not just words.
entries.16:1: God is about to give Ezekiel a message. It shows that what follows is not Ezekiel's own idea but words that came directly from God.
entries.16:2: God tells Ezekiel to confront Jerusalem openly about its shameful behavior. The reader should understand that God does not ignore wrong doing but names it plainly.
entries.16:3: Jerusalem's origins were among the Canaanite peoples, not from a noble or holy background. The city owed nothing to its own heritage; it began as an outsider.
entries.16:4: A newborn in that world was normally cleaned, rubbed with salt, and wrapped in cloths. Jerusalem is pictured as a baby nobody bothered to care for at all.
entries.16:5: No one felt sorry for this abandoned baby or showed it any kindness; it was thrown out into open country because it was unwanted. The picture is of complete rejection and helplessness.
entries.16:6: God passed by and saw the baby lying in its own blood, and he commanded it to live. The reader should see that life came as God's gift, not from anything the child deserved.
entries.16:7: God made the abandoned child grow and flourish like plants in a field until she reached adulthood. She became mature, yet she was still naked and uncovered, with no one to care for her.
entries.16:8: When God saw she had reached the age for love, he covered her nakedness, made a solemn promise, and entered into a covenant with her. She became his, bound to him by his own commitment.
entries.16:9: God cleaned her up, washing away the blood of her birth and soothing her with oil. This shows his tender care in making her clean and whole.
entries.16:10: God dressed her in fine embroidered cloth, leather shoes, linen, and silk. Every good thing she wore was a gift from him, not something she earned.
entries.16:11: God adorned her with jewelry, bracelets, and a necklace. He was making her beautiful and treating her like someone precious.
entries.16:12: God added a nose ring, earrings, and a beautiful crown. The crown especially shows that he gave her honor and dignity.
entries.16:13: She became stunning, dressed in gold, silver, and the finest fabrics, and fed with the best food. Her beauty and comfort all came from God's generosity.
entries.16:14: Her beauty became famous among the nations, but it was God's splendor given to her that made her beautiful. The reader should not mistake God's gifts for personal achievement.
entries.16:15: Instead of trusting God, she trusted her own beauty and used her fame to chase after anyone who passed by. She took the gifts meant for a relationship with God and threw them away.
entries.16:16: She used the fine clothes God gave her to build colorful shrines for false worship. She turned gifts meant for good into tools for unfaithfulness.
entries.16:17: She melted down the silver and gold God had given her and made idols shaped like men. She gave God's own gifts to things that were not God.
entries.16:18: She dressed her idols in the embroidered robes God had given her and offered his oil and perfume to them. The very things meant for honoring God were used to honor false gods.
entries.16:19: She took the fine food God provided and burned it as offerings to idols. She gave to false gods what God had given her to eat.
entries.16:20: She even took the children God had given her and offered them to idols as food. This is one of the darkest charges in the passage.
entries.16:21: She killed God's own children and passed them through fire as sacrifices to idols. The reader should feel the horror of trading what God loves for what he hates.
entries.16:22: Through all of this she never remembered how helpless she once was, lying in her blood with no one to help. Forgetting where you came from leads to terrible ingratitude.
entries.16:23: God declares that after all this evil there is still more to come. The list of charges is not finished.
entries.16:24: She built shrines in public squares for her false worship. Her unfaithfulness was open and shameless, not hidden.
entries.16:25: She set up shrines at every street corner and used her beauty to lure passersby into sin. She offered herself to anyone and multiplied her unfaithfulness.
entries.16:26: She pursued Egypt, her powerful neighbor, and gave herself to them, making God angry. She looked to other nations instead of to God.
entries.16:27: God stretched out his hand against her, reduced her provision, and handed her over to those who hated her. Even her enemies were shocked by how far she had gone.
entries.16:28: She went after Assyria too, driven by desires that could never be satisfied. Sin kept promising more but never delivered.
entries.16:29: She carried her unfaithfulness all the way to Babylonia and still was not satisfied. No amount of chasing other lovers filled the emptiness.
entries.16:30: God calls her heart weak and shameless for doing all these things like a brazen woman. Her behavior showed a heart that had stopped listening to God.
entries.16:31: She built shrines at every street and public place, yet she was unlike a prostitute because she refused payment. She gave herself away freely, which made it worse.
entries.16:32: She is like a wife who cheats on her husband and takes other lovers in his place. The image is of betrayal against someone who had every right to her loyalty.
entries.16:33: Normally people pay prostitutes, but she paid her lovers to come to her. She reversed the natural order, spending herself to buy betrayal.
entries.16:34: She was different from other women because no one pursued her; she paid them instead. Her sin was not driven by need but by a restless, self-destructive heart.
entries.16:35: God addresses her directly as an unfaithful woman and calls her to listen to his word. Judgment is coming, and she needs to hear it.
entries.16:36: God lists the reasons for judgment: her shameless unfaithfulness, her idols, and the blood of her children sacrificed to them. Nothing was hidden from God.
entries.16:37: God will gather all her lovers and even those she hated to come against her from every side, and she will be exposed before them. Those she trusted will become the ones who shame her.
entries.16:38: God will judge her like an unfaithful wife and a murderer, pouring out his anger and jealousy. His judgment is described in the strongest terms.
entries.16:39: God will hand her over to her lovers, who will tear down her shrines, strip her of her clothes and jewels, and leave her exposed and ashamed. The gifts she misused will be taken away.
entries.16:40: A crowd will gather against her to stone her and cut her down with swords. This pictures the violent end that her betrayal brings.
entries.16:41: The city will be publicly punished and destroyed in front of many onlookers, and its shameful behavior will finally stop. It means wrongdoing eventually ends, but not without consequences.
entries.16:42: God's anger will finally run its course and then stop, and he will be calm again. It means God's anger is real but not endless; there comes a point when it is over.
entries.16:43: They forgot how good things were when they were young and instead kept doing things that provoked God, so the results of their choices will fall on them. It means forgetting past kindness and repeating wrong behavior brings its own consequences.
entries.16:44: People will sum up the situation with a common saying: a daughter turns out like her mother. It means people are judged by the family pattern they follow.
entries.16:45: They are just like their mother and sisters, who rejected their husbands and children, and their family roots were foreign and pagan. It means they inherited and repeated a pattern of unfaithfulness.
entries.16:46: Samaria to the north and Sodom to the south are called their older and younger sisters, each with dependent towns. It means these neighboring peoples are close relatives in guilt, not strangers.
entries.16:47: They did not just copy their sisters' wrongs; they went further and became worse in everything they did. It means copying bad examples can lead to outdoing them.
entries.16:48: God swears by his own life that Sodom never did the wicked things Jerusalem and its towns have done. It means Jerusalem's guilt is worse than the famous city of Sodom.
entries.16:49: Sodom's sin was pride, too much food, comfortable wealth, and refusing to help the poor and needy. It means plenty and comfort without generosity is serious wrongdoing.
entries.16:50: They became proud and did disgusting things before God, so he removed them. It means arrogance and shameless behavior bring judgment.
entries.16:51: Samaria did not commit even half of Jerusalem's sins, and Jerusalem's many wrongs made her sisters look almost innocent by comparison. It means our wrongs can be worse than those we look down on.
entries.16:52: Jerusalem must be ashamed because her sins were worse than her sisters', making them seem upright by comparison. It means being worse than those we condemn should bring deep shame.
entries.16:53: God promises to restore Sodom, Samaria, and Jerusalem alike. It means God's mercy can reach even those who seem most ruined.
entries.16:54: Jerusalem will feel shame and humiliation when God shows mercy to her despite all she has done. It means mercy can make us see our wrong more clearly.
entries.16:55: Sodom, Samaria, and Jerusalem will all be restored to how they were at first. It means God can bring back what was lost and ruined.
entries.16:56: When Jerusalem was proud, she used Sodom as a warning on her lips. It means we easily condemn others while ignoring our own faults.
entries.16:57: Now Jerusalem's own shame is exposed, and she has become a disgrace among neighboring peoples like Edom and the Philistines. It means the judgment we pronounce on others can fall on us.
entries.16:58: The results of their wicked plans and disgusting behavior have come back on them, says the Lord. It means we reap what we have done.
entries.16:59: God will treat them as they treated him, because they set aside their oath and broke the agreement. It means breaking a promise to God has real consequences.
entries.16:60: Yet God will remember the agreement he made with them long ago and will establish an everlasting agreement. It means God's faithfulness outlasts our failures.
entries.16:61: Remembering their ways will fill them with shame when God gives them their sisters as daughters, not because of any agreement on their part. It means God's grace is not earned by us.
entries.16:62: God will make his agreement with them, and they will know for certain that he is the Lord. It means a restored relationship leads to truly knowing God.
entries.16:63: Remembering all this will leave them speechless with shame, because God has forgiven everything they did, says the Lord. It means real forgiveness produces humble, quiet gratitude.
entries.17:1: God is about to speak to the prophet Ezekiel. This reminds the reader that what follows is a message from God, not just a man's opinion.
entries.17:2: God tells Ezekiel to tell the people a riddle and a story with a hidden meaning. The reader should expect a picture that stands for something real.
entries.17:3: A huge eagle with colorful feathers comes to Lebanon and takes the top of a cedar tree. This eagle stands for a powerful king who takes away the leaders of a nation.
entries.17:4: The eagle carries off the top young branch to a land of traders and plants it in a city of merchants. This means the captured leaders were taken away to a foreign trading city.
entries.17:5: The eagle takes some seed from the land and plants it in good soil near plenty of water, like a willow. This means he set up a weak ruler to grow under his control.
entries.17:6: The seed grows into a low, spreading vine that leans toward the eagle. This means the new ruler stayed small and dependent on the king who put him there.
entries.17:7: Another great eagle appears, and the vine turns its roots and branches toward him for water. This means the ruler looked to another powerful nation for help instead of staying loyal.
entries.17:8: The vine had been planted in good ground with plenty of water so it could grow strong and bear fruit. The reader sees that it had every chance to thrive where it was.
entries.17:9: God asks whether this vine will prosper, then says its roots will be pulled up and its branches cut off so it dries out. This means the disloyal ruler will be uprooted and ruined.
entries.17:10: Even if the vine is replanted, the hot east wind will dry it up where it grows. This means no amount of replanting will save it from coming destruction.
entries.17:11: God speaks to Ezekiel again. This marks a new step in the message, moving from the riddle to its meaning.
entries.17:12: God tells Ezekiel to explain the riddle to a stubborn people: the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and carried its king and officials away to Babylon. The reader learns the story is about real events.
entries.17:13: The king of Babylon made a treaty with a member of the royal family, put him under oath, and removed the leading men of the land. This means he set up a puppet ruler bound by a promise.
entries.17:14: The treaty was meant to keep the kingdom weak so it could not rise up and would stay loyal. The reader sees that the arrangement was designed to keep the nation under control.
entries.17:15: But that ruler rebelled and sent messengers to Egypt asking for horses and a large army. God asks whether someone who breaks an agreement like that can succeed or stay safe.
entries.17:16: God swears by his own life that the ruler will die in Babylon, the place of the king who made him king, because he broke his oath and treaty. Breaking a solemn promise brings serious consequences.
entries.17:17: Pharaoh with his strong army will not help him when the enemy builds siege works and walls to destroy lives. The reader sees that relying on a foreign power will fail.
entries.17:18: He broke the agreement even though he had given his hand to it, so he will not escape safely. The reader learns that a broken pledge, even to a pagan king, is not ignored.
entries.17:19: God says that because the ruler set aside the oath and agreement made in God's name, God will punish him. The reader sees that promises made before God matter deeply.
entries.17:20: God will spread his net over him, catch him, bring him to Babylon, and judge him there for his wrong against God. The reader sees that no one escapes God's judgment.
entries.17:21: His best soldiers will be killed and the rest scattered to every direction, and then people will know the Lord has spoken. The reader sees that God's word comes true.
entries.17:22: God says he himself will take a tender top shoot from the high cedar and plant it on a high and great mountain. This means God will start a new, humble kingdom himself.
entries.17:23: It will be planted on the high mountain of Israel, grow branches, bear fruit, and become a beautiful cedar where birds of every kind nest in its shade. The reader sees a picture of a safe, fruitful kingdom that blesses many.
entries.17:24: All the trees will see that the Lord brings down the high tree and lifts up the low one, dries the green tree and makes the dry one grow. The reader learns that God is the one who controls who rises and who falls.
entries.18:1: God is speaking directly to the prophet Ezekiel, giving him a message to pass on to the people. It reminds the reader that God still speaks and cares enough to correct his people.
entries.18:2: The people were quoting a proverb saying children suffer for their parents' sins, like teeth aching after parents ate sour grapes. It means they blamed their ancestors for their troubles instead of taking responsibility themselves.
entries.18:3: God swears by his own life that this proverb will stop being used in Israel. It means God will not let his people keep blaming others for their own situation.
entries.18:4: Every person belongs to God, parent and child alike, and each one is accountable for their own sin. It means you are responsible for your own choices, not someone else's.
entries.18:5: God describes a person who lives rightly and does what is fair. It means real goodness shows up in how a person lives day to day.
entries.18:6: This person avoids idol worship and sexual sins that God had forbidden. It means being faithful to God includes keeping our bodies and worship pure.
entries.18:7: This person treats others fairly, returns what is owed, refuses to rob anyone, and shares food and clothing with the needy. It means honest dealings and generosity are marks of a good life.
entries.18:8: This person refuses to profit by charging interest on loans and stays honest in business. It means we should not take advantage of people who are struggling.
entries.18:9: Someone who follows God's rules faithfully will live, God says. It means obedience to God leads to life, not just knowing the rules but doing them.
entries.18:10: If that good man has a son who becomes a thief or a killer, the son is not good just because of his father. It means you cannot borrow your parents' goodness; each person stands on their own.
entries.18:11: This son copies none of his father's good ways but instead commits the same sins God forbade. It means a good family background does not excuse bad choices.
entries.18:12: He oppresses the poor, robs people, refuses to repay debts, and worships idols. It means mistreating the vulnerable and betraying God are serious wrongs.
entries.18:13: He lends money to make a profit off others, and God says he will not live. It means greed that harms people brings judgment, and the person alone bears the blame.
entries.18:14: But if this man's son sees his father's sins and chooses not to repeat them, that matters. It means you can break a bad family pattern by choosing differently.
entries.18:15: This grandson avoids the idol worship and sexual sins his father committed. It means you are not doomed to copy the sins of your family.
entries.18:16: He does not oppress anyone, takes nothing by force, and gives food and clothing to those in need. It means kindness and fairness are choices each person can make.
entries.18:17: He keeps his hands clean, refuses dishonest profit, and follows God's commands. It means he will not die for his father's sins but will live because of his own right choices.
entries.18:18: His father, however, was cruel and violent and did evil among his people, so he will die for his own sin. It means each person's wrongdoing catches up with them personally.
entries.18:19: The people ask why the son does not suffer for the father's sin. God answers that a son who does what is right will live. It means God judges each person by their own conduct.
entries.18:20: The one who sins is the one who dies; children are not punished for parents' sins or parents for children's. It means guilt and credit belong to the individual who acted.
entries.18:21: If a wicked person turns from all their sins and starts obeying God, they will live. It means it is never too late to change, and God accepts a real turnaround.
entries.18:22: None of their past sins will be held against them once they turn. It means God forgives genuinely, not keeping a record of what you did before.
entries.18:23: God says he takes no pleasure in the death of a wicked person but wants them to turn and live. It means God's heart is for people to change, not to be destroyed.
entries.18:24: If a righteous person turns away and does evil, their past good deeds will not save them. It means you cannot coast on past goodness; what matters is where you are now.
entries.18:25: The people accuse God's way of being unfair. God turns it around and asks whether their own ways are the unfair ones. It means we often blame God when the problem is our own choices.
entries.18:26: When a righteous person turns to evil, they die for that evil. It means turning away from good has real consequences, no matter how good your past was.
entries.18:27: When a wicked person turns from evil and does what is right, they will live. It means a genuine change of direction brings life, whatever came before.
entries.18:28: Because they saw their wrong and turned from it, they will live and not die. It means recognizing your sin and leaving it is the path to life.
entries.18:29: Israel keeps saying God's way is unfair, but God insists their own ways are the unfair ones. It means we can be quick to accuse God while ignoring our own faults.
entries.18:30: God will judge each person by their own ways and calls them to turn from their sins. It means the time to change is now, before sin brings you down.
entries.18:31: God tells them to throw off their sins and get a new heart and spirit, asking why they would choose death. It means God wants you to want life, and he invites you to start fresh.
entries.18:32: God says he takes no pleasure in anyone's death and pleads with them to turn back and live. It means God's deepest desire for you is life, not judgment.
entries.19:1: God tells Ezekiel to sing a sad funeral song about the kings of Israel. It means the reader should hear this as mourning for leaders who fell, not as a happy poem.
entries.19:2: The mother lion stands for Israel and its royal family, raising up princes among the nations. It means the reader should see the nation pictured as a mother proud of her cubs.
entries.19:3: One cub grew into a young lion that hunted people, meaning a king became violent and oppressive. It means the reader should see that power used to harm others brings trouble.
entries.19:4: Other nations heard about him and trapped him, dragging him to Egypt with hooks. It means the reader should see that a violent ruler was captured and taken away in shame.
entries.19:5: When the mother saw her hope was gone, she raised another cub to be a young lion. It means the reader should see the nation trying again with another king after the first was taken.
entries.19:6: This second cub also became a fierce young lion that hunted people. It means the reader should see the same pattern of violence repeating in the next ruler.
entries.19:7: He destroyed widows and ruined towns, and the land was laid waste by his roaring. It means the reader should see that a ruler's cruelty brings ruin on ordinary people and the whole country.
entries.19:8: Nations from all around came against him and caught him in their net. It means the reader should see that such a ruler is finally surrounded and trapped by his enemies.
entries.19:9: They put him in a cage with hooks and took him to Babylon, so his voice was no longer heard in Israel. It means the reader should see that the loud, destructive king was silenced and exiled.
entries.19:10: The mother is compared to a vine planted by water, fertile and full of branches. It means the reader should see that Israel once had life and strength given by God.
entries.19:11: She had a strong branch fit for a ruler's scepter, towering high among the branches. It means the reader should see that the nation once had real royal power and honor.
entries.19:12: But she was pulled up in anger and thrown down, and the east wind dried her up and fire burned her branches. It means the reader should see that pride and God's judgment brought the nation low.
entries.19:13: Now she is planted in a dry, unwatered wasteland. It means the reader should see the nation living in exile, cut off from the life it once had.
entries.19:14: Fire came out from her branch and burned up her branches, leaving no scepter for a ruler; this is a song of grief. It means the reader should see that the royal line was destroyed, and the song is meant to be mourned.
entries.20:1: Some of Israel's leaders came to the prophet Ezekiel to ask God what they should do, and they sat down in front of him. It shows that people can go through the motions of seeking God while their hearts are still far from him.
entries.20:2: God spoke to Ezekiel at that moment. The message that follows is not Ezekiel's own opinion but words that came directly from God.
entries.20:3: God tells Ezekiel to confront these leaders: they have come asking for guidance, but God refuses to answer them. Coming to God for advice while holding on to sin does not work.
entries.20:4: God asks Ezekiel whether he is willing to judge these leaders, then tells him to lay out plainly the shameful history of their ancestors. Sometimes people need to see the past clearly before they can understand their own problem.
entries.20:5: God reminds them of the day he chose Israel and made a promise to Jacob's descendants, revealing himself to them in Egypt and pledging to be their God. It is a reminder that their relationship with God began with his initiative, not theirs.
entries.20:6: On that same day God swore to bring them out of Egypt into a rich, good land he had picked out for them. God's promises include both rescue from slavery and a future worth having.
