entries.20:7: God told them to throw away the vile idols they were drawn to and to stop defiling themselves with Egypt's images, because he alone was their God. The first thing God asked of them was to turn from what they were clinging to.
entries.20:8: But they rebelled, refused to listen, and would not give up their idols, so God was ready to pour out his anger on them right there in Egypt. Stubborn refusal to let go of sin provokes God's judgment.
entries.20:9: God held back for the sake of his own reputation, so his name would not be disgraced in front of the nations who had watched him reveal himself by rescuing Israel. God's honor, not Israel's worthiness, moved him to act.
entries.20:10: So God did bring them out of Egypt and led them into the wilderness. He kept his promise even though they had not deserved it.
entries.20:11: God gave them his laws and instructions, which would bring life to anyone who kept them. His rules were meant to be a gift that leads to life, not a burden.
entries.20:12: God also gave them the Sabbaths as a sign between him and them, showing that he is the one who makes them holy. Rest and worship were meant to mark them as God's own people.
entries.20:13: But in the wilderness the Israelites rebelled too, ignoring God's rules and Sabbaths, so God was ready to destroy them there. The same stubbornness that showed up in Egypt continued in the wilderness.
entries.20:14: Again God acted to protect his own name from being disgraced in the eyes of the nations who had seen him bring Israel out. God's reputation among the nations mattered to him.
entries.20:15: God also swore in the wilderness that that generation would not enter the good land he had promised them. Their rebellion cost them the very gift God had prepared.
entries.20:16: The reason was that they turned away from God's rules and Sabbaths and their hearts chased after idols. What the heart loves determines where a person ends up.
entries.20:17: Even so, God looked on them with pity and did not destroy them completely in the wilderness. His mercy held back the full judgment they deserved.
entries.20:18: God warned the next generation in the wilderness not to follow their fathers' rules or defile themselves with their fathers' idols. Each generation is invited to break the pattern rather than repeat it.
entries.20:19: God told them plainly that he is the Lord their God, and they should follow his rules and keep his commands. The call is personal: obey me, not the example of your parents.
entries.20:20: They were to keep the Sabbaths holy as a sign between God and them, so they would know he is their God. Setting apart time for God helps people remember whose they are.
entries.20:21: But that generation rebelled too, ignoring God's life-giving rules and Sabbaths, so God was ready to pour out his anger on them in the wilderness. The pattern of rebellion repeated itself.
entries.20:22: Once more God held back for the sake of his name, so it would not be disgraced before the nations. God's mercy and his reputation again spared them.
entries.20:23: God also swore in the wilderness that he would scatter them among the nations and drive them out among other countries. Exile was a warned consequence, not a surprise.
entries.20:24: The reason was that they rejected God's rules and Sabbaths and set their hearts on their fathers' idols. Rejecting God's ways leads to being uprooted.
entries.20:25: God gave them over to rules that were not good and orders that brought no life. When people insist on rejecting what is good, God can let them live with the harmful consequences of their choice.
entries.20:26: He let them become defiled through their offerings, even to the point of sacrificing their firstborn children in fire, until they were ruined. This shows how far people sink when God stops restraining them.
entries.20:27: God tells Ezekiel to confront Israel again: their ancestors added further shame to God's name by being unfaithful to him. Sin is not just a private matter; it dishonors God.
entries.20:28: When God brought them into the promised land, they used every high hill and leafy tree as a place to offer sacrifices that stirred his anger. They turned God's gift into an occasion for idolatry.
entries.20:29: God asked them what this high place they kept going to was really worth, and it has been called Bamah ever since. Their worship at these places was empty and pointless.
entries.20:30: God asks the present generation whether they intend to defile themselves the way their fathers did and chase the same disgusting practices. The question forces them to see that they are repeating the family pattern.
entries.20:31: They were still offering sacrifices and making their sons pass through fire, yet they expected God to give them direction. God swears he will not answer them. You cannot keep sinning and expect God to guide you.
entries.20:32: They wanted to become just like the surrounding nations, serving idols of wood and stone, but God says that plan will never happen. God will not let his people simply dissolve into the world around them.
entries.20:33: God swears that with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and poured-out anger, he will be King over them. He will rule them whether they like it or not.
entries.20:34: God will gather them out of the countries where they have scattered, using that same strong hand and fierce anger. His discipline and his rescue come with the same power.
entries.20:35: God will bring them into a wilderness among the peoples and there deal with them face to face. He intends a direct, personal reckoning, not a distant one.
entries.20:36: Just as God judged their fathers in the wilderness on the way from Egypt, so he will judge them. The past is a warning picture of what is coming.
entries.20:37: God will make them pass under the shepherd's rod, counting and examining each one, and will reduce their number. He will sort out who truly belongs to him.
entries.20:38: God will remove from among them those who rebel and sin against him; they will leave the land where they live but will not enter Israel, and then they will know he is the Lord. Not everyone who claims a place among God's people will share in the promise.
entries.20:39: God tells Israel to go ahead and put away their idols and listen to him, so his holy name is no longer shamed by their offerings and images. The choice is set before them plainly: drop the idols and listen, or keep dishonoring God.
entries.20:40: On God's holy mountain, the high mountain of Israel, all the people will serve him there; he will accept them and be pleased with their offerings and firstfruits. After judgment comes a promise of restored worship and acceptance.
entries.20:41: God says He will be pleased with His people like a pleasing smell when He brings them home from exile. For the reader, it means God's rescue of His people is something He delights in, not something He does reluctantly.
entries.20:42: When God brings them back to the land He promised their ancestors, they will know for certain that He is the Lord. For the reader, it means God keeps His promises, and His faithfulness shows people who He really is.
entries.20:43: Once they are home, remembering their past sins and defilement will make them hate themselves for the evil they did. For the reader, it means real repentance includes feeling genuine sorrow over sin, not making excuses for it.
entries.20:44: God will act to restore them for the sake of His own name and honor, not because their behavior deserved it. For the reader, it means God's mercy rests on His character and reputation, not on how good we are.
entries.20:45: This line simply introduces a new message that God gave to the prophet Ezekiel. For the reader, it shows that what follows is God speaking, not just the prophet's own idea.
entries.20:46: God tells Ezekiel to face south and speak His message against the forest land of the south. For the reader, it means God's warnings are directed at specific places and people, not vague generalities.
entries.20:47: God says He will start a fire in that forest that burns both green and dry trees and cannot be put out, scorching the whole land from south to north. For the reader, it means God's judgment is thorough and unstoppable when people refuse to listen.
entries.20:48: Everyone will see that the Lord Himself started this fire, and it will not be quenched. For the reader, it means God's judgment is public and unmistakable, so no one can claim it was just an accident.
entries.20:49: Ezekiel protests that people already think he only speaks in riddles and stories. For the reader, it means God's messengers can face mockery, and even faithful words may be dismissed as mere talk.
entries.21:1: God is speaking directly to Ezekiel, giving him a message to pass on. It reminds the reader that what follows is not Ezekiel's own opinion but words God gave him.
entries.21:2: God tells Ezekiel to face Jerusalem and speak his message of judgment toward the temple and the whole land of Israel. The prophet must deliver a hard word to God's own people, not just to outsiders.
entries.21:3: God says he is now against Israel and will use war to cut off both good and bad people alike. When judgment comes on a nation, no one escapes its effects.
entries.21:4: Because both good and bad will be cut off, God's sword of judgment will sweep across the whole land from south to north. The coming disaster will reach everyone, not just a few.
entries.21:5: Everyone will see that God himself has brought this judgment, and it will not be put away until it is finished. God's warnings are not empty threats.
entries.21:6: God tells Ezekiel to groan openly with a broken heart in front of the people. The prophet's visible grief is part of the message, showing how serious the coming disaster is.
entries.21:7: When people ask why he is groaning, Ezekiel is to say it is because of news that is coming, which will make everyone's courage melt and strength fail. The fear will be so great that even strong people will be terrified.
entries.21:8: God speaks to Ezekiel again, introducing the next part of his message. It marks a new section of the prophecy.
entries.21:9: God tells Ezekiel to announce that a sword has been sharpened and polished, ready for use. The image shows that judgment is prepared and about to fall.
entries.21:10: The sword is sharpened to kill and polished so it flashes like lightning. The picture stresses how deadly and sudden the coming judgment will be.
entries.21:11: God has handed the sword to a craftsman to sharpen and polish it, then it will be placed in the hand of the one who kills. God is in control of the instrument of judgment.
entries.21:12: Ezekiel is to cry out and mourn because the sword is coming on God's people and their rulers. Even God's own people will not be spared, so grief is the right response.
entries.21:13: This verse says that the testing will surely come, and the sword of judgment will strike even the leader of God's people. For the reader, it means no one is exempt from God's correction, and His warnings are serious rather than empty threats.
entries.21:14: God tells Ezekiel to clap his hands and announce that the sword will strike again and again, a great sword of slaughter that surrounds the people. The repeated blows show the judgment will be severe and widespread.
entries.21:15: The purpose of this terror is to make hearts melt and to increase the number of the fallen, with the sword set against every gate. The judgment is meant to break down resistance and bring many down.
entries.21:16: The sword is told to turn to the right and left, striking wherever it is directed. Nothing is safe from its path.
entries.21:17: God himself will clap his hands and bring his anger to rest once the judgment is done. The judgment is real, but it has an end, and God is the one who controls it.
entries.21:18: God speaks to Ezekiel once more, beginning another part of the message. It signals a new scene in the prophecy.
entries.21:19: Ezekiel is told to mark out two roads for the king of Babylon's army, both starting from the same land, with a signpost where they split. The picture shows a real military campaign being planned.
entries.21:20: One road leads to Rabbah of Ammon and the other to Judah and Jerusalem. The signpost shows the enemy has a choice of which city to attack first.
entries.21:21: At the fork in the road, the king of Babylon uses divination, shaking arrows and consulting his idols and inspecting an animal's liver, to decide which way to go. Even a pagan king's decision-making is shown here as part of how events unfold.
entries.21:22: The divination points to Jerusalem, so the king orders an attack with battle cries, siege engines, earthworks, and walls. The decision means Jerusalem will be the target of the assault.
entries.21:23: To the people of Jerusalem who had sworn oaths, this omen will seem like a false sign, but the king remembers their wrongdoing and will seize them anyway. Their broken promises will be used against them.
entries.21:24: God says that because their wrongdoing has been exposed and brought to mind, they will be caught in it. Hidden sin eventually becomes visible and has consequences.
entries.21:25: God addresses the wicked ruler of Israel, who is doomed, saying his day of final punishment has come. The leader who should have protected the people is himself under judgment.
entries.21:26: God says the ruler's turban and crown must be removed, and the social order will be reversed: the low lifted up and the high brought down. Pride and power are being stripped away.
entries.21:27: God declares the kingdom will be overturned again and again until the rightful king comes, and then God will give it to him. The collapse is not the end; God has a future ruler in mind.
entries.21:28: God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Ammon too, saying a sword is drawn and polished for slaughter, flashing like lightning. Ammon is not exempt from judgment either.
entries.21:29: The visions and divinations of Ammon's false prophets are worthless, giving false comfort to doomed evildoers whose day of punishment has come. False assurances cannot stop God's judgment.
entries.21:30: God tells Ammon's sword to go back into its sheath, because he will judge them in their own land where they came from. There is no escape from God's judgment, even at home.
entries.21:31: God will pour out his burning anger on them and hand them over to brutal men trained to destroy. The judgment is described as fierce and carried out by violent people.
entries.21:32: They will be burned up, their blood poured out in their own land, and their memory erased, because God has spoken. The judgment ends in total ruin and being forgotten.
entries.22:1: God is speaking directly to the prophet Ezekiel. This verse simply sets up the message that follows, showing that what comes next is from God, not from Ezekiel himself.
entries.22:2: God asks Ezekiel whether he is willing to confront the city of Jerusalem, which is guilty of murder. He is told to spell out clearly to the city all the wrong things it has done.
entries.22:3: God says Jerusalem has killed people and made idols, and this is bringing its day of judgment closer. The city's own violence and idol worship are what set up its downfall.
entries.22:4: Jerusalem is guilty of the blood it shed and the idols it made, and this has brought its judgment time near. As a result, God will make the city a disgrace and a joke among the nations.
entries.22:5: People both nearby and far away will mock Jerusalem. Its name will be ruined, and it will be full of panic and fear.
entries.22:6: The leaders of Israel have each used their power to cause death in the city. Those meant to protect people have instead been harming them.
entries.22:7: In Jerusalem people have shown no respect for parents, have mistreated foreigners, and have wronged orphans and widows. God sees how the vulnerable are being treated badly.
entries.22:8: The people have treated God's holy things as unimportant and have not kept the Sabbath holy. They have dishonored what God set apart for himself.
entries.22:9: In the city there are people who slander others and cause death, who eat meat with blood still in it, and who carry out wicked plans openly. Wrongdoing has become normal in the streets.
entries.22:10: People in Jerusalem have committed shameful sexual sins, including dishonoring their parents and mistreating a woman during her monthly period. These acts break God's laws about purity and family.
entries.22:11: One man has committed a disgusting sin with his neighbor's wife, another has wronged his daughter-in-law, and another has sinned with his own sister. Sexual sin has spread even within families.
entries.22:12: People have taken bribes to kill, charged unfair interest, and stolen from neighbors by force, and they have forgotten God. Greed and violence have replaced any memory of the Lord.
entries.22:13: God claps his hands in anger at the violence and bloodshed in Jerusalem. He is showing that he will not ignore what the city has done.
entries.22:14: When God acts against them, the people will not be brave or strong enough to resist. What God has said he will do, he will do.
entries.22:15: God will scatter the people among other nations and remove the uncleanness from among them. Being spread out among the nations becomes part of how God cleanses them.
entries.22:16: The city will be humbled in front of other nations, and then the people will know that God is the Lord. Their humiliation will make God's identity clear.
entries.22:17: God is again speaking to the prophet Ezekiel. This line introduces the next message God gives him.
entries.22:18: God says the people of Israel have become like worthless scrap metal, a mix of metals with no value. They are no longer precious to him the way silver would be.
entries.22:19: Because the people have become worthless metal, God says he will gather them together inside Jerusalem. The gathering is for judgment, not for safety.
entries.22:20: Just as metals are put in a furnace and melted by fire, God will gather his people and melt them down in his anger. His wrath will be like the fire that softens the metal.
entries.22:21: God will breathe his fiery anger onto the people, and they will soften under it. They will not be able to stand firm against his judgment.
entries.22:22: As silver melts in a furnace, so the people will melt under God's anger. Then they will know that the Lord has poured out his fury on them.
entries.22:23: God speaks to Ezekiel once more. This verse begins another message from the Lord.
entries.22:24: God describes the land as one that has received no rain or storm on the day of wrath. It is a picture of a land left dry and without blessing.
entries.22:25: The leaders are like a roaring lion tearing at its prey, devouring people and seizing wealth and property. Their greed has left many widows behind.
entries.22:26: The priests have broken God's law and treated holy things as unclean, failing to teach the difference between holy and common. They have ignored the Sabbaths, so God is not honored among the people.
entries.22:27: The officials are like wolves tearing at their prey, killing people and destroying lives to make a profit. Their leadership is driven by greed.
entries.22:28: The prophets cover up the truth with false assurances, claiming visions and messages that did not come from God. They say the Lord has spoken when he has not.
entries.22:29: The ordinary people have also been cruel, using force to take what belongs to others and oppressing the poor, the needy, and foreigners. The wrongdoing is not only among leaders but throughout the land.
entries.22:30: God looked for even one person who would stand in the gap and defend the land before him, but he found no one. There was nobody willing to intercede and turn the people back.
entries.22:31: So God poured out his anger and brought the consequences of the people's ways down on their own heads. Their punishment matched what they had done.
entries.23:1: God is speaking to Ezekiel and giving him a message. This reminds the reader that what follows is not Ezekiel's own idea but a message from God.
entries.23:2: God tells a story about two women who came from the same mother, meaning two sister cities or nations. It sets up a picture of two peoples who shared the same origin.
entries.23:3: These two women had already been sexually immoral back in Egypt when they were young. This pictures how these peoples were unfaithful to God from early in their history.
entries.23:4: The two women are named Oholah and Oholibah, and God says they belonged to him and had children. The names stand for Samaria and Jerusalem, the capitals of the two kingdoms.
entries.23:5: Oholah, meaning Samaria, was unfaithful to God and chased after the Assyrians, a powerful neighboring nation. It shows how that kingdom looked to other nations for help and love instead of trusting God.
entries.23:6: She was drawn to the Assyrians because they looked impressive, dressed in fine blue clothes and riding horses. The reader sees that outward splendor can tempt people to turn away from God.
entries.23:7: She gave herself to the best men of Assyria and also worshiped their idols. This means the people joined in the sins and false worship of the nations around them.
entries.23:8: She never stopped the immoral ways she had learned in Egypt long before. It shows that old habits of unfaithfulness can carry on for generations if not dealt with.
entries.23:9: So God handed her over to the Assyrians she had desired. This means God let her suffer the consequences of the very things she chased after.
entries.23:10: The Assyrians exposed her shame, killed her children, and put her to death, and other women heard about it. This pictures how Samaria was destroyed and became a warning to others.
entries.23:11: Her sister Oholibah, meaning Jerusalem, saw all this but was even more reckless in her unfaithfulness. It warns that seeing someone else's downfall does not automatically stop us from doing worse.
entries.23:12: She too chased after the Assyrians because they looked impressive and powerful. Again, the pull of outward show led her away from God.
entries.23:13: God saw that she had become unclean and that both sisters were walking the same wrong path. It shows that following the same sins leads to the same ruin.
entries.23:14: Her unfaithfulness got even worse: she saw pictures of Babylonian men painted on a wall and was drawn to them. It shows how a picture or image can stir up wrong desires.
entries.23:15: The men in the pictures looked like Babylonian rulers, with belts and headdresses. She was attracted to their status and appearance.
entries.23:16: As soon as she saw them, she wanted them and sent messengers to Babylon. It shows how quickly desire can turn into action.
entries.23:17: The Babylonians came and were intimate with her, and afterward she turned away from them in disgust. This means she got what she wanted but was left empty and ashamed.
entries.23:18: Her shameful behavior was plain to see, and God turned away from her just as he had from her sister. It shows that persistent unfaithfulness makes God withdraw his closeness.
entries.23:19: Even so, she kept going deeper into immoral behavior, remembering her early days in Egypt. It shows how she kept returning to old patterns of sin.
entries.23:20: She desired her lovers with raw physical lust, described in crude terms. This pictures how out of control and degraded her craving for other nations had become.
entries.23:21: She kept bringing back memories of her early immoral days in Egypt. It shows that she longed for the old sinful life instead of turning back to God.
entries.23:22: So God says he will bring against her the very lovers she had turned away from in disgust. This means the nations she once wanted will become the ones who punish her.
entries.23:23: God lists the Babylonians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians who will come against her, all impressive fighting men on horseback. It shows that a great army is coming as God's instrument of judgment.
entries.23:24: They will come from the north with chariots and many troops, fully armed, and will judge her. This means a powerful invasion will bring God's verdict against her.
entries.23:25: God's anger will work against her through these attackers, who will mutilate her and kill her children and burn what is left. This pictures the brutal destruction that will come.
entries.23:26: They will strip off her clothes and take away her jewelry. This means her wealth and beauty will be taken from her, leaving her exposed and humiliated.
entries.23:27: God will put an end to her evil ways that came from Egypt, and she will never look back to them again. It shows that God's judgment aims to stop the sin for good.
entries.23:28: God says he will hand her over to the nations she hates and turns from in disgust. This means the ones she once rejected will become her masters.
entries.23:29: Those nations will treat her with hatred, take away everything she worked for, and leave her naked and ashamed. It shows the full cost of her unfaithfulness.
entries.23:30: All this happens because she was unfaithful to God and joined herself to other nations and their idols. It makes clear that the punishment comes from her own choices.
entries.23:31: She followed the same path as her sister, so God will give her the same cup of judgment. It means she will share the same fate.
entries.23:32: She will drink from her sister's cup, which is deep and wide, and she will be mocked and despised more than she can bear. This pictures a heavy and humiliating judgment.
entries.23:33: That cup will bring her brokenness and sorrow, the same ruin that came on Samaria. It means she will experience the same devastation her sister did.
entries.23:34: She will drink it all down to the last drop and tear at her own breasts in grief. This pictures total ruin and deep despair.
entries.23:35: Because she forgot God and turned her back on him, she will bear the punishment for her evil and immoral ways. It shows that ignoring God brings its own consequences.
entries.23:36: God tells Ezekiel to confront Oholibah and spell out the disgusting things she has done. It shows that God's messenger must speak plainly about sin.
entries.23:37: She was unfaithful to God, guilty of bloodshed, and worshiped idols, even burning her own children as offerings. This shows how far her rebellion had gone.
entries.23:38: She also defiled God's holy place and broke his Sabbaths. It means she treated what God set apart as sacred with contempt.
entries.23:39: Right after sacrificing her children to idols, she came into God's house and made it unclean. It shows shocking hypocrisy, mixing worship with terrible sin.
entries.23:40: She even sent for men from far away, washing and painting herself and dressing up to attract them. This pictures how she eagerly prepared herself for unfaithfulness.
entries.23:41: She sat on a fancy bed with a table set before her and used God's own perfume and oil there. It means people took what belonged to God and used it for their own pleasure, and it warns us not to misuse what God has given us.
entries.23:42: She was dressed up with jewelry and crowns to look attractive for her lovers. It means outward show was used to cover up unfaithfulness, and it reminds us that God sees past appearances.
entries.23:43: God said she would just keep going in her loose ways. It means sin becomes a habit that people don't stop on their own, and it warns us that unchecked wrong behavior only grows.
entries.23:44: Men came to her the way men visit a prostitute. It means she was fully given over to her unfaithfulness, and it shows how far people can drift when they turn from God.
entries.23:45: Upright men will judge her as an unfaithful wife and a murderer, because she was untrue to God and had blood on her hands. It means betrayal of God and violence against others bring real judgment, and it reminds us that wrongs are not ignored.
entries.23:46: God said he would bring a great crowd against her to terrify her and strip her of everything. It means the consequences of her sin would come through other people, and it shows that God's warnings are serious.
entries.23:47: The crowd would stone her, kill her with swords, put her children to death, and burn her house. It means her whole life and family would be destroyed by judgment, and it shows how devastating the results of persistent sin can be.
entries.23:48: God would stop the evil in the land and teach all women not to copy her example. It means judgment also serves as a warning to others, and it reminds us that our choices affect more people than just ourselves.
entries.23:49: God would bring the punishment her evil ways deserved, and she would know he is the Lord. It means sin finally meets its consequences and God is shown to be true to his word, and it calls us to take him seriously.
entries.24:1: God gave Ezekiel a message on one specific day, and the exact date is recorded. It shows that what follows is tied to a real moment in history, not a vague story.
entries.24:2: God told Ezekiel to write down that same day, because Babylon's army had just begun its attack on Jerusalem. The point for the reader is that God knows and announces events as they happen, not after the fact.
entries.24:3: God told Ezekiel to tell a story about a cooking pot to a people who would not listen. The pot on the fire stands for Jerusalem, and the story is a picture of what is coming.
entries.24:4: The best pieces of meat and the best bones go into the pot, meaning the leading people of the city. The picture is that no one important will escape what is coming.
entries.24:5: The fire is piled high and the pot is left to boil until everything in it is cooked. It means the destruction will be complete, not partial.
entries.24:6: God calls Jerusalem a city of blood, like a pot so dirty inside that it can never be cleaned. The message is that the city's guilt is deep and its judgment is certain.
entries.24:7: The city's violence was done openly, like blood poured on bare rock instead of being covered with dirt. It means the wrongdoing was shameless and could not be hidden.
entries.24:8: God let the blood stay out in the open on purpose, so that the wrong would be seen and answered. It means injustice does not go unnoticed by God.
entries.24:9: God repeats the charge and says he himself will make the fire burn hotter. The reader should see that God takes the city's violence personally and will act.
entries.24:10: The fire is fed, the meat is boiled down, and even the bones are burned. It means the judgment will leave nothing standing.
entries.24:11: The empty pot itself is put on the coals until its filth is burned away. The picture is that the city's uncleanness must be removed, even if it takes fire to do it.
entries.24:12: God says he has worn himself out trying to clean the pot, but the filth remains and still stinks. It means the people kept resisting every chance to change.
entries.24:13: God wanted to cleanse his people, but they refused, so now the cleansing will come through judgment instead. The reader learns that refusing to be made clean has consequences.
entries.24:14: God says he will do exactly what he said, without changing his mind or holding back. It means his warnings are not empty threats.
entries.24:15: This line simply introduces the next message God gave Ezekiel. It marks a new scene in the story.
entries.24:16: God told Ezekiel that his wife, the one he loved most, would suddenly die, and he was not to mourn openly. It shows how costly the prophet's role as a sign to the people would be.
entries.24:17: Ezekiel was told to go on with normal life, wearing his turban and sandals and eating regular food, instead of doing the usual grieving. It means his strange calm was itself a message to the people.
entries.24:18: Ezekiel preached to the people in the morning, his wife died that evening, and the next morning he did exactly as God commanded. It shows his obedience even at great personal cost.
entries.24:19: The people noticed his odd behavior and asked him what it meant. It shows that his actions made them stop and pay attention.
entries.24:20: Ezekiel begins his answer by saying the message came from God, not from himself. It reminds the reader that the explanation is God's, not the prophet's own idea.
entries.24:21: God said he would let his own temple be defiled, the very thing the people were most proud of, and their children left behind would be killed. It means even their most treasured things would not protect them.
entries.24:22: The people would act just as Ezekiel did, without the usual signs of mourning. It means their grief would be too deep and too shocking for normal expressions.
entries.24:23: They would keep their turbans and sandals on and not weep, but waste away under the weight of their sin. It means life would go on outwardly while they were dying inside.
entries.24:24: Ezekiel himself became a living sign, and when his words came true the people would know God was real. It means God uses ordinary lives to prove his word is true.
entries.24:25: God told Ezekiel that on the day the people lost everything they treasured, including their children, his own mouth would be shut. It means he would have nothing more to say until the news arrived.
entries.24:26: On that day a survivor would escape and come to Ezekiel with the news. It means the report of the disaster would finally reach him.
entries.24:27: When the survivor came, Ezekiel would speak again and no longer be silent, and the people would know God was behind it all. It means his silence and his speech together were proof of God's word.
entries.25:1: God spoke directly to Ezekiel, giving him a message to deliver. It reminds the reader that what follows is God's own word, not Ezekiel's opinion.
entries.25:2: God told Ezekiel to face the Ammonites, a neighboring nation, and speak God's message against them. It shows that God's words reach beyond Israel to other peoples too.
entries.25:3: The Ammonites had mocked and celebrated when God's temple was defiled, Israel's land was ruined, and Judah's people were taken captive. God says they will answer for rejoicing over another nation's disaster.
entries.25:4: Because of their mockery, God will hand the Ammonites' land over to people from the east, who will settle there and consume its produce. It means their security and wealth will be taken by outsiders.
entries.25:5: Their capital city will become pasture for camels and their land a resting place for sheep. The outcome will make clear that God, not their idols, is truly Lord.
entries.25:6: God accuses the Ammonites of clapping, stamping, and rejoicing with deep contempt when Israel fell. It warns that delighting in someone else's downfall is not harmless.
entries.25:7: So God will stretch out his hand against them, let their wealth be plundered, and remove them from among the nations. Their destruction will show that God is the Lord.
entries.25:8: Moab and Seir (Edom) were saying that Judah was no different from any other nation. They dismissed God's special people and, in effect, dismissed God's promises.
entries.25:9: God will expose Moab's flank, leaving its border towns—its proudest places—open to attack. Even a nation's strongest defenses cannot stand when God acts against it.
entries.25:10: God will give Moab, along with Ammon, to the people of the east so that Moab will no longer be remembered among the nations. It means lasting loss of identity and place.
entries.25:11: God himself will judge Moab, and the result will show everyone that he is the Lord. Justice belongs to God, not to the nations who mocked his people.
entries.25:12: Edom took revenge on Judah and so became deeply guilty. God treats unjust vengeance against his people as a serious wrong.
entries.25:13: God will act against Edom, cutting off its people and animals and making the land desolate from Teman to Dedan. It means total judgment across the whole nation.
entries.25:14: God will use Israel to pay Edom back for what it did, and Edom will feel his anger. It shows God defends his people and settles accounts with those who harm them.
entries.25:15: The Philistines acted out of endless hatred, seeking to shame and destroy Judah. God sees motives, not just actions, and unending malice draws his judgment.
entries.25:16: God will stretch out his hand against the Philistines, cutting off the Cherethites and destroying the rest of the coastal people. It means their power along the sea will come to an end.
entries.25:17: God will punish them in fierce anger, and they will know that he is the Lord when his judgment falls. It reminds the reader that God's justice is real and will not be ignored.
entries.26:1: This verse simply dates when God gave Ezekiel this message, during the eleventh year of the exile. It reminds the reader that these words are tied to a real moment in history, not a vague legend.
entries.26:2: The city of Tyre celebrated when Jerusalem fell, treating its ruin as good news and a chance for profit. It warns us that gloating over someone else's downfall invites God's attention.
entries.26:3: God says he is personally against Tyre and will bring many nations against it, like waves rolling in one after another. It shows that no powerful city stands outside God's reach.
entries.26:4: Tyre's walls and towers will be torn down, and the city will be scraped bare like a flat rock. What seemed unshakeable can be reduced to nothing.
entries.26:5: The city will become a bare rock where fishermen spread their nets, and its wealth will go to other nations. A great trading center will be reduced to a fishing spot.
entries.26:6: The towns around Tyre on the mainland will be killed in war, and everyone will then know that God is real. Judgment will be so clear that no one can miss who caused it.
entries.26:7: God names the instrument of judgment: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, coming from the north with a huge army. It shows God can use even a pagan king to carry out his purposes.
entries.26:8: The nearby towns will be killed, and the enemy will build siege walls and ramps against the city. It describes the slow, terrifying tightening of a siege.
entries.26:9: The attacker will bring battering rams and weapons against the walls and knock down the towers. No defense will hold against what God has decreed.
entries.26:10: The sheer number of horses will raise so much dust that the city is covered, and the walls will shake at the noise of chariots coming through the gates. It pictures overwhelming force that cannot be stopped.
entries.26:11: Enemy horses will trample the streets, people will be killed, and the city's strong pillars will fall to the ground. The proud city's strength will be flattened.
entries.26:12: The attackers will loot all the wealth and trade goods, tear down houses, and throw the rubble into the sea. Even the city's remains will be dumped into the water.
entries.26:13: God will silence the city's music and songs. The joy and celebration of a rich city will be cut off completely.
entries.26:14: Tyre will become a bare rock where nets are spread, never to be rebuilt. God himself guarantees it, so the outcome is certain.
entries.26:15: Coastal nations will tremble at the sound of Tyre's collapse and the cries of its wounded. One city's fall will shake everyone who depended on it.
entries.26:16: The rulers of sea-trading nations will step down from their thrones, take off their fine clothes, sit on the ground trembling, and be stunned at what happened. The mighty will be humbled by Tyre's fate.
entries.26:17: They will sing a funeral song for Tyre, mourning how the famous strong city and its people, who once terrified everyone, have been destroyed. Even great powers are mourned and then gone.
entries.26:18: Coastal lands will tremble on the day Tyre falls, and every ship's crew will be terrified. The shock will spread to everyone connected to the sea trade.
entries.26:19: God will make Tyre a deserted ruin like cities no one lives in, and great waters will cover it. The city will be swallowed up as if by the sea.
entries.26:20: God will send Tyre down to the world of the dead, to join people long gone, never to be lived in again or share in the land of the living. It is a picture of total, final removal.
entries.26:21: Tyre will become a horror and come to a complete end, so thoroughly gone that no one will ever find it again. God's word says its disappearance will be permanent.
entries.27:1: God spoke to Ezekiel again with a new message. It reminds the reader that God keeps speaking and directing his prophet.
entries.27:2: God tells Ezekiel to sing a funeral song over the city of Tyre. It means Tyre's end is certain, like singing at a funeral before the death happens.
entries.27:3: Tyre sat by the sea and grew rich trading with many nations, and it proudly called itself perfectly beautiful. The reader sees how pride in wealth and beauty invites God's judgment.
entries.27:4: Tyre's builders made it like a splendid ship built out at sea. Its beauty and strength came from human skill, not from God.
entries.27:5: The ship was built with fine wood from distant mountains, using fir for the planks and cedar for the masts. This shows how Tyre drew the best materials from everywhere.
entries.27:6: Its oars and deck were made of costly oak and ivory from faraway lands. The picture stresses how much wealth went into making Tyre magnificent.
entries.27:7: Its sails were fine embroidered linen from Egypt and its awnings were blue and purple cloth. Even the smallest details of Tyre's beauty came from expensive trade.
entries.27:8: Skilled sailors from nearby coastal cities steered Tyre's ships. Tyre depended on experts from many places to keep its trade moving.
entries.27:9: Experienced craftsmen from Gebal repaired the ship, and sailors from everywhere came to trade in Tyre's goods. The city was the hub of a vast network of skilled workers and merchants.
entries.27:10: Soldiers from distant African lands served in Tyre's army and made it look glorious. Tyre's splendor was propped up by hired foreign troops.
entries.27:11: Soldiers from Arvad guarded Tyre's walls and towers with their weapons. The city trusted in its defenses and hired guards to make itself seem secure and beautiful.
entries.27:12: Tarshish traded with Tyre because of its huge wealth, swapping silver, iron, tin, and lead for its goods. Tyre's riches drew trade from far across the sea.
entries.27:13: Greece and nearby lands traded with Tyre, exchanging slaves and bronze vessels for its goods. The reader sees that Tyre's prosperity was built on commerce, even in human lives.
entries.27:14: Togarmah traded horses and mules to Tyre for its goods. Many nations brought what Tyre wanted in exchange for its products.
entries.27:15: Rhodes and many island peoples traded with Tyre, paying with ivory and ebony. Tyre's reach stretched across the sea-lands.
entries.27:16: Edom traded with Tyre because of its many manufactured goods, giving jewels, purple cloth, fine linen, coral, and rubies. Tyre's industry attracted luxury goods from many regions.
entries.27:17: Judah and Israel traded with Tyre, supplying grain, honey, oil, and perfume. Even God's own people were caught up in Tyre's trading network.
entries.27:18: Damascus traded with Tyre because of its great wealth, exchanging wine and white wool. Tyre's riches made it a center for trade with inland cities too.
entries.27:19: Iron and spices were also exchanged for Tyre's goods. The list keeps showing how many different products flowed through Tyre.
entries.27:20: Dedan traded with Tyre in cloths used for saddling horses. Even distant desert traders did business with the wealthy city.
entries.27:21: Arabia and the rulers of Kedar traded lambs, sheep, and goats with Tyre. Tyre's markets drew livestock from the desert peoples.
entries.27:22: Sheba and Raamah traded with Tyre, bringing the finest spices, precious stones, and gold. The richest goods of the world flowed into Tyre.
entries.27:23: Haran, Canneh, Eden, Asshur, and the Medes also traded with Tyre. The list shows that nearly every major trading region dealt with this city.
entries.27:24: These traders brought beautiful robes, blue cloth, embroidered goods, and cedar chests tied with cords. Tyre was a marketplace for the finest goods of the ancient world.
entries.27:25: Ships from Tarshish carried Tyre's goods, and the city became full and glorious on the sea. Its success seemed complete and unshakable.
entries.27:26: But Tyre's sailors took it into deep waters, and a strong east wind broke it apart at sea. The very trade that made Tyre great became the setting for its ruin.
entries.27:27: On the day of its downfall, all Tyre's wealth, goods, sailors, craftsmen, traders, and soldiers will sink into the sea together. Nothing the city trusted in will save it.
entries.27:28: When the ship's guides cry out, the ship's planks will shake. The sound of panic shows how sudden and total the collapse will be.
entries.27:29: All the sailors and sea experts will leave their ships and stand on the shore. Those who once worked for Tyre will step back and watch it fall.
entries.27:30: They will cry loudly over Tyre, throw dust on their heads, and roll in the dust. This is the ancient way of showing deep grief and mourning.
entries.27:31: They will shave their heads and wear rough cloth, weeping with bitter sorrow for Tyre. The city's fall will cause real, painful mourning among those who knew it.
entries.27:32: In their grief they will sing a funeral song, asking who could compare to Tyre, now destroyed in the sea. The once-great city will become a warning.
entries.27:33: Tyre's exports filled many peoples and made the kings of the earth rich. Its trade blessed many, but that success did not protect it from judgment.
entries.27:34: Now Tyre is broken in the deep waters, and its goods and people sink with it. The same sea that carried its wealth becomes the place of its ruin.
entries.27:35: Everyone in the sea-lands is shocked at Tyre's fall, and its kings are terrified and troubled. The mighty city's collapse will shake the whole region.
entries.27:36: The traders among the peoples gasp in surprise at Tyre, which has become a thing of horror and ended forever. The reader is warned that pride and wealth cannot stand against God's judgment.
entries.28:1: God is about to give Ezekiel another message. It shows that what follows comes directly from God, not from Ezekiel himself.
entries.28:2: God tells Ezekiel to confront the ruler of Tyre, who has become so proud he thinks he is a god sitting on a divine throne. The point for the reader is that no human, however powerful, is actually God.
entries.28:3: God mocks the ruler's belief that he is wiser than Daniel and knows every secret. It warns against thinking our knowledge makes us superior to everyone else.
entries.28:4: The ruler used his cleverness and knowledge to gain power and pile up silver and gold. It's a reminder that skill and success can easily become the foundation of pride.
entries.28:5: His wealth grew through trade and wisdom, and his heart became proud because of his own power. Success itself isn't the problem; letting it make us arrogant is.
entries.28:6: God announces judgment because the ruler has set his heart up as if he were God. It shows how seriously God takes human pride.
entries.28:7: God will bring fierce foreign armies against him, and they will destroy his prized wisdom and glory. Whatever we build on pride can be stripped away by forces beyond our control.
entries.28:8: They will kill him and send him down to the grave, dying like any ordinary person. It shows that even the mightiest ruler ends up in the same place as everyone else.
entries.28:9: When killers are closing in, he will still claim to be a god, but he will be exposed as a mere man. It's a picture of how powerless pride is when real trouble comes.
entries.28:10: He will die at the hands of foreigners, a shameful death for someone who claimed divinity. God's word is certain, and no claim of greatness can cancel it.
entries.28:11: God speaks to Ezekiel again, introducing a new message. It marks a fresh word from God about the same king.
entries.28:12: God tells Ezekiel to sing a funeral song over the king of Tyre, describing him as perfectly wise and beautiful. It's irony: the one who seemed so magnificent is being mourned before he falls.
entries.28:13: The king is pictured as if he had been in Eden, dressed in every precious gem, with gold prepared for him from the start. It shows how richly God had blessed him, which makes his pride even more tragic.
entries.28:14: He is described as a guardian angel figure placed on God's holy mountain, walking among fiery stones. It stresses that his high position was a gift from God, not something he earned.
entries.28:15: He was blameless from the day he was created until evil was found in him. It teaches that sin entered something that had started out good.
entries.28:16: His dishonest trading filled him with violence, so God drove him out of his honored place in disgrace. It shows that corrupt dealings can cost us everything we were given.
entries.28:17: His beauty made him proud, and his wisdom was ruined by his sin, so God brought him down to earth for kings to see. It warns that pride turns our best gifts into our downfall.
entries.28:18: His sinful trading defiled his sanctuaries, so God will burn him up and reduce him to dust for all to see. It shows that sin eventually destroys the sinner himself.
entries.28:19: Everyone who knew him will be shocked, and he will be gone forever. It's a sober picture of how complete and final the fall of the proud can be.
entries.28:20: God begins another message through Ezekiel. It signals a shift from Tyre to a new target.
entries.28:21: God tells Ezekiel to face the city of Sidon and prophesy against it. It shows God's judgment is not limited to one nation.
entries.28:22: God declares himself against Sidon and will show his glory by judging it, so people will know he is the Lord. Even judgment serves to reveal who God truly is.
entries.28:23: Disease and bloodshed will fill Sidon's streets, with enemies attacking from every side, and people will recognize God's hand in it. It's a vivid warning that God sees and answers evil.
entries.28:24: Israel will no longer be pricked and troubled by hostile neighbors who shamed them. It promises relief for God's people from constant harassment.
entries.28:25: God promises to gather Israel back from the nations and show his holiness through them, and then they will live in the land he gave Jacob. It's a promise of restoration after exile.
entries.28:26: They will live securely, building homes and planting vineyards without fear, once God judges their mocking neighbors, and they will know him as their God. It pictures the peace that comes when God sets things right.
entries.29:1: This verse simply dates the moment when God gave Ezekiel a message, tying it to a specific year, month, and day. It reminds the reader that God's words came at real, recorded times in history, not as vague legend.
entries.29:2: God tells Ezekiel to face the king of Egypt and speak a prophetic warning against him and the whole nation. It means God was about to address Egypt directly, and the reader should see that no powerful nation is outside God's notice.
entries.29:3: God pictures Pharaoh as a huge river creature lying in the Nile, boasting that the river belongs to him and he made it for himself. It means pride in what we claim to own puts us against God, who made everything.
entries.29:4: God says he will hook this creature and drag it and all the fish out of the river. It means Pharaoh's power and everything that depended on him will be pulled down and exposed, not left safe in the water.
entries.29:5: The creature and its fish will be thrown on dry ground to die and become food for wild animals and birds. It means Egypt's downfall will be total and public, with no proper burial or honor.
entries.29:6: Everyone in Egypt will know God is real because Egypt proved to be a false support to Israel. It means relying on a powerful ally instead of God ends in disappointment, and God will be shown to be the true support.
entries.29:7: Egypt was like a staff that splintered when Israel leaned on it, cutting their hands and breaking their arms. It means trusting a shaky power hurts the one who trusts it, not just the one who fails.
entries.29:8: Because of this, God says he will bring war on Egypt and cut off both people and animals. It means the false support will be judged, and the reader should take God's warning about misplaced trust seriously.
entries.29:9: Egypt will become an empty wasteland, and people will know God is real because Pharaoh claimed the Nile as his own. It means boasting about what we did not create leads to loss, and God will be recognized in the end.
entries.29:10: God says he is against Egypt and its rivers and will make the whole land desolate from one end to the other. It means the judgment will be complete, covering the entire country, not just a part.
entries.29:11: No person or animal will pass through the land, and it will stay empty for forty years. It means the devastation will be long and thorough, a full generation of emptiness.
entries.29:12: Egypt will be laid waste like other ruined nations, and its people will be scattered among the countries for forty years. It means the proud nation will be humbled and its people displaced, just as God said.
entries.29:13: After forty years, God promises to gather the Egyptians back from the nations where they were scattered. It means judgment has a limit, and God still shows mercy and restores people after discipline.
entries.29:14: God will restore Egypt's fortunes and bring them back to their homeland, but there they will be a weak, unimportant kingdom. It means restoration comes, but the old pride and power will not return.
entries.29:15: Egypt will be the lowest of kingdoms and will never again rule over other nations, because God will make it small. It means God keeps proud powers from rising again, and the reader should not envy or fear them.
entries.29:16: Egypt will no longer be Israel's hope, and looking to it will only remind them of their sin; then they will know God is real. It means God removes false hopes so his people learn to trust him alone.
entries.29:17: This verse gives another exact date when God's message came to Ezekiel, years after the earlier one. It means God's plans unfold over time, and he keeps speaking and working through history.
entries.29:18: Babylon's king worked his army hard against Tyre, wearing out their heads and arms, but got no payment from it. It means even a pagan king's labor is seen by God, and hard work deserves a real reward.
entries.29:19: So God gives Egypt to Babylon's king, who will carry off its wealth as payment for his army. It means God can use any ruler to carry out his purposes, and he settles accounts in his own way.
entries.29:20: God says he gave Egypt to Babylon as a reward because the army was working for God's purposes. It means God is in charge of history, and even nations that don't know him end up serving his plan.
entries.29:21: On that day God will give Israel new strength and let Ezekiel speak freely among them, and they will know God is real. It means after judgment comes hope, and God's people will see his power and hear his word again.
entries.30:1: God spoke to Ezekiel again, giving him a new message. This shows that God keeps speaking and guiding his prophet step by step.
entries.30:2: God tells Ezekiel to speak as his messenger and to cry out in shock about the coming day of judgment. The reader should take God's warnings seriously rather than treat them lightly.
entries.30:3: A day of the Lord is coming soon, a dark day of trouble that will affect many nations. It reminds the reader that God does act in history and holds nations accountable.
entries.30:4: War will strike Egypt, and neighboring Ethiopia will be terrified as Egypt's people fall and its wealth is carried off. The reader sees that no nation's strength or riches can protect it from God's judgment.
entries.30:5: Many allied peoples and regions will fall together with Egypt by the sword. This shows that those who tie themselves to a doomed power share in its downfall.
entries.30:6: God says Egypt's supporters will collapse and its proud strength will be brought low, with people killed throughout the land. The reader learns that pride in power is fragile before God.
entries.30:7: Egypt will become a desolate ruin among other ruined lands, its towns left empty. This pictures the total emptiness that follows when God brings a nation down.
entries.30:8: When God sets Egypt on fire and breaks its helpers, people will know that he is the Lord. Judgment is meant to make God's reality and authority unmistakable.
entries.30:9: Messengers will hurry out in ships to terrify Ethiopia, which felt safe, and its people will be in anguish because the same disaster is coming to them. The reader sees that no one who feels secure is beyond God's reach.
entries.30:10: God says he will use Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, to cut down Egypt's large population. God can use even a foreign ruler to carry out his purposes.
entries.30:11: Nebuchadnezzar and his fierce army will be sent to destroy Egypt, and their swords will fill the land with the dead. The reader sees that God's judgment is carried out through real, terrifying events.
entries.30:12: God will dry up Egypt's rivers and hand the land over to foreigners who will ruin it. Even the natural sources of life are under God's control, and he confirms he will do it.
entries.30:13: God will destroy Egypt's idols and false gods, end its line of rulers, and fill the land with fear. The reader learns that false gods cannot save a nation when the true God acts.
entries.30:14: God will make several Egyptian regions desolate and send fire and punishment on their cities. The judgment is specific and widespread, showing God's thoroughness.
entries.30:15: God will pour out his anger on a strong Egyptian city and cut off its many people. The reader sees that even the strongest places cannot stand against God's wrath.
entries.30:16: God will set Egypt on fire, and its cities will writhe in pain or be broken apart like a flood. This pictures the sudden, overwhelming nature of the coming disaster.
entries.30:17: The young men of two Egyptian cities will be killed, and the towns themselves will be taken captive. The reader sees that the next generation and the cities' future are cut off.
entries.30:18: A dark day will come to another Egyptian city when Egypt's control is broken and its pride ends, with its people carried away. The reader learns that God brings down proud power and leaves it in darkness.
entries.30:19: God will punish Egypt, and then people will know that he is the Lord. The purpose of the judgment is that God's identity and authority be recognized.
entries.30:20: This verse gives the exact date when God's message came to Ezekiel. It shows the prophecy is tied to real history, not a vague story.
entries.30:21: God says he has already broken the arm of Pharaoh, Egypt's king, and no one has bandaged it so he can fight again. The reader sees that Egypt's military power has been crippled by God himself.
entries.30:22: God declares he is against Pharaoh and will break his other arm too, taking the sword from his hand. The reader learns that opposing God means losing all strength to resist.
entries.30:23: God will scatter the Egyptians among the nations so they wander from country to country. This shows the result of judgment is displacement and loss of home.
entries.30:24: God will strengthen Babylon's king and put his sword in his hand, while Pharaoh's arms are broken and he cries out in pain. God is the one directing who rises and who falls.
entries.30:25: God will make Babylon strong and leave Pharaoh's arms hanging weak, and people will know that he is the Lord when Babylon's sword is raised against Egypt. The reader sees God's hand behind the events of nations.
entries.30:26: God will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and they will know that he is the Lord. Even in exile and loss, the purpose is that people recognize God's power.
entries.31:1: This verse simply marks the date when God gave Ezekiel a message, showing that the prophet's words were tied to real history. It reminds the reader that God speaks at specific times and places, not in vague generalities.
entries.31:2: God tells Ezekiel to confront Pharaoh and Egypt with a pointed question: who do you think you compare to in your power? It invites the reader to examine whether pride in strength is ever justified.
entries.31:3: Egypt is pictured as a magnificent, towering tree with lush branches that seemed to reach the sky. The image shows how impressive and secure the nation looked to everyone watching.
entries.31:4: The tree grew huge because of abundant water flowing around and out from it. This means Egypt's greatness came from resources and conditions it did not create, a reminder that power is often a gift rather than an achievement.
entries.31:5: Fed by those waters, the tree outgrew every other tree in the field. The point is that Egypt rose above other nations, and the reader is meant to see how easily success breeds a sense of superiority.
entries.31:6: Birds nested in its branches, animals gave birth under it, and great nations lived in its shade. This shows that Egypt's power drew many peoples to depend on it, much like a strong country today attracts allies and dependents.
entries.31:7: The tree was beautiful because its roots reached deep, plentiful water. Its beauty rested on hidden sources of strength, reminding the reader that outward splendor often depends on things we cannot see.
entries.31:8: Even the finest trees in God's garden could not match it. The comparison is meant to show that Egypt's glory seemed unmatched, yet it was still measured against God's own standard.
entries.31:9: God himself made the tree beautiful, and the other trees envied it. The reader should notice that the greatness was God-given, so boasting about it makes no sense.
entries.31:10: Because the tree grew tall and its heart became proud, God announces judgment. The lesson is that pride in one's height or success invites a fall.
entries.31:11: God hands the proud tree over to a powerful foreign nation to be punished for its sin. It shows that no amount of strength protects anyone from the consequences of arrogance.
entries.31:12: Foreign invaders cut the tree down and left it lying across the mountains and valleys, and the peoples who once sheltered under it walked away. The picture is of a great nation suddenly abandoned by everyone who depended on it.
entries.31:13: Now only birds sit on the fallen trunk and wild animals stand on its branches. What was once a home for many has become a ruin, showing how complete the reversal is.
entries.31:14: God's purpose is that no well-watered tree should ever again lift itself up in pride, because all of them are destined for death like every human being. It reminds the reader that no nation, however prosperous, escapes mortality.
entries.31:15: When the tree goes down to the world of the dead, God makes the deep waters mourn and the forests grow dark. Creation itself grieves over the fall of something so great, which shows the seriousness of the loss.
entries.31:16: Nations shake at the sound of its fall, while the other trees of Eden take comfort that even this giant came down. The reader learns that the downfall of the proud is a warning and, oddly, a comfort to those who remain.
entries.31:17: Its helpers and those who lived under its shade go down with it to the place of the dead. Dependence on a powerful patron does not save anyone when that patron falls.
entries.31:18: God closes by asking Pharaoh who he thinks he is like, then declares that he and all his people will be brought down to the lowest place among the dead. The message is blunt: Egypt's splendor ends in the grave, and the reader is warned not to trust in earthly glory.
entries.32:1: This dates the message: God spoke to Ezekiel on a specific day in the twelfth year of exile. It shows these warnings were real events at a real time, not vague legends.
entries.32:2: God tells Ezekiel to sing a funeral song over Pharaoh, who acted like a powerful beast thrashing the waters and muddying them for everyone. It means proud leaders who stir up trouble will finally be brought down.
entries.32:3: God says he will trap Pharaoh like a fisherman catching a great sea creature in a net. No matter how powerful a person seems, God can bring them to a stop.
entries.32:4: Pharaoh will be dragged out and left on the ground for birds and wild animals to feed on. It pictures total humiliation for someone who once seemed untouchable.
entries.32:5: The picture grows grimmer: his remains will be scattered over mountains and fill the valleys. It stresses how complete his downfall will be.
entries.32:6: His blood will soak the land and fill the streams. The point is that his defeat will affect the whole land, not just himself.
entries.32:7: When Pharaoh falls, the sky itself will seem to go dark—sun, moon, and stars hidden. It's a picture of deep gloom and disaster surrounding his end.
entries.32:8: God says all the lights in the sky will go dark over Egypt's land. It means the nation's downfall will feel like darkness covering everything.
entries.32:9: Many peoples will be shaken when they hear of Egypt's fall and see its captives scattered among foreign nations. News of such a collapse spreads fear far beyond Egypt.
entries.32:10: Kings will be stunned and tremble with fear for their own lives when they see what happened to Pharaoh. It's a warning that no ruler is safe from the same kind of judgment.
entries.32:11: God names the tool of judgment: the king of Babylon's army will attack Egypt. God uses even foreign empires to carry out his purposes.
entries.32:12: Babylon's fierce soldiers will cut down Egypt's people and destroy the nation's pride. Human strength and pride offer no protection when God decides to act.
entries.32:13: God will wipe out Egypt's livestock along the great waters, and the waters will no longer be stirred up by people or animals. Even the land's ordinary life will come to a halt.
entries.32:14: After the destruction, God will let the waters settle and run smooth like oil. It shows that calm and order can return only after judgment has done its work.
entries.32:15: When Egypt is left empty and everyone in it is punished, people will know that God is the Lord. The purpose of the judgment is to make God's reality unmistakable.
entries.32:16: This funeral song will be sung by mourning women of many nations for Egypt and its people. It shows that Egypt's fall will be widely lamented, not ignored.
entries.32:17: This gives another date for a second message, two weeks after the first one. It marks a separate word from God about Egypt's fate.
entries.32:18: God tells Ezekiel to wail loudly and picture Egypt going down to the grave with the other nations. It means Egypt will join the ranks of the fallen, not escape death.
entries.32:19: Egypt is asked whether it is any better than the others, then told to go down and lie among the uncircumcised dead. Pride about beauty or status means nothing in the grave.
entries.32:20: Egypt will lie among those killed by the sword, along with all its people. The nation's fate is the same as everyone else's who falls in battle.
entries.32:21: The mighty dead already in the grave will mockingly welcome Egypt to join them among the slain. Even in death, Egypt's pride is exposed as empty.
entries.32:22: Assyria is shown lying in the grave with its whole army, all killed by the sword. Once-fearsome empires end up in the same place.
entries.32:23: Assyria's graves are deep in the underworld, though it once spread terror among the living. Past power and fear do not save anyone from death.
entries.32:24: Elam is there too, killed by the sword and shamed among the dead, despite once causing fear. The same humbling end awaits every proud nation.
entries.32:25: Elam has a resting place among the dead with all its people, shamed like the rest. It reinforces that no nation escapes this common fate.
entries.32:26: Meshech and Tubal lie there with their people, killed by the sword, though they too once terrified the living. Their former strength is now meaningless.
entries.32:27: These are buried with ancient warriors who took their weapons to the grave, still feared in their day. Even honored fighters end up among the dead.
entries.32:28: Egypt is told it will lie among the uncircumcised, killed by the sword, just like the others. It will share the same humbling end as every other nation.
entries.32:29: Edom's kings and princes are there too, resting among the slain and the uncircumcised. High rank does not change where they end up.
entries.32:30: The northern chiefs and the Sidonians are there, shamed despite the fear their strength once caused. Their power did not protect them from death or disgrace.
entries.32:31: Pharaoh will see all these others in the grave and be comforted about his own army's fate. It's a grim comfort: he is not alone in his downfall.
entries.32:32: Though Pharaoh spread fear among the living, he will lie among the uncircumcised, killed by the sword, with all his people. God's word is clear that his terror ends in the grave.
entries.33:1: God spoke directly to Ezekiel, giving him a message to pass on. It reminds us that God still speaks and uses people to deliver what he says.
entries.33:2: God tells Ezekiel to picture a country that appoints a lookout to warn people of an approaching army. The point is that someone must be on guard and speak up when danger comes.
entries.33:3: When the lookout sees the enemy coming, he blows a warning horn so everyone can hear. The warning gives people a chance to get to safety.
entries.33:4: If someone hears the warning but ignores it, that person bears the blame for their own death. Ignoring a clear warning is a choice with real consequences.
entries.33:5: Because they heard the warning and did nothing, they are responsible for their own fate. If they had acted on the warning, they would have lived.
entries.33:6: If the lookout fails to warn anyone, the people still die for their own sins, but God holds the lookout accountable for not speaking up. Failing to warn others is serious.
entries.33:7: God appoints Ezekiel as a lookout for Israel, responsible for hearing God's words and warning the people. God still calls people to speak his truth to those around them.
entries.33:8: If God announces judgment on a wicked person and Ezekiel stays silent, the wicked person dies, but God holds Ezekiel responsible for not warning them. Staying silent when we should speak carries its own guilt.
entries.33:9: If Ezekiel warns the wicked person and they still refuse to change, they die for their own sin, but Ezekiel is not to blame. Our job is to warn faithfully; the response is up to the other person.
entries.33:10: The people complain that their sins are crushing them and ask how they can possibly live. Guilt can make people feel hopeless, but God is about to answer that despair.
entries.33:11: God swears that he takes no pleasure in anyone's death and longs for wicked people to turn from their ways and live. God's heart is for people to change and be saved, not to punish.
entries.33:12: Past goodness won't protect someone who now does wrong, and past wrongdoing won't doom someone who now turns from it. What matters is the direction of your life now, not your record.
entries.33:13: If a righteous person trusts in their own goodness and starts doing evil, their past good deeds won't save them. No one can rest on past obedience while living wrongly.
entries.33:14: If God warns a wicked person of death and they turn from their sin and do what is right, there is hope. Change is always possible while there is time.
entries.33:15: Real change shows itself in action: returning what was taken, paying debts, and following God's ways. Genuine repentance produces a changed life, and such a person will live.
entries.33:16: When a wicked person turns and does right, God forgives and forgets their past sins. God's forgiveness is complete, not partial.
entries.33:17: The people accuse God of being unfair, but it is actually their own ways that are crooked. It's easy to blame God when the real problem is ourselves.
entries.33:18: If a righteous person turns away and does evil, they will die for that evil. Turning from good has real consequences.
entries.33:19: If a wicked person turns from evil and does what is right, they will live. Turning toward good brings life.
entries.33:20: The people still claim God is unfair, but God will judge each person by their own ways. God's judgment is fair because it deals with what each person actually does.
entries.33:21: A refugee from Jerusalem arrived with news that the city had fallen. This confirmed the judgment God had warned about through Ezekiel.
entries.33:22: The night before the refugee arrived, God opened Ezekiel's mouth, ending his period of silence. God prepared him to speak again at exactly the right moment.
entries.33:23: God gave Ezekiel another message to deliver. God keeps speaking to his people even after judgment has come.
entries.33:24: The people left in the land claimed it as their own because Abraham once received it, and they were many. They assumed God's promise guaranteed them the land no matter how they lived.
entries.33:25: God points out their sins—eating meat with blood, idol worship, and murder—and asks whether such people deserve the land. Claiming God's promises while living in disobedience is empty.
entries.33:26: They relied on their swords, did detestable things, and committed adultery, yet still expected the land. Trusting in your own strength while ignoring God's standards doesn't earn his blessing.
entries.33:27: God declares that those in the ruins will fall by the sword, those in the open will be eaten by wild animals, and those hiding in caves will die of disease. Judgment will reach everyone, wherever they hide.
entries.33:28: God will make the land desolate and strip away its pride, leaving the mountains empty and untraveled. Sin leads to ruin even for a land once blessed.
entries.33:29: When the land lies waste, the people will finally recognize God for who he is. Sometimes it takes loss to open our eyes to God's reality.
entries.33:30: The people talk about Ezekiel by the walls and doorways, urging each other to come hear God's word. They were curious about the message but not committed to it.
entries.33:31: They come and sit as if they are God's people and listen to Ezekiel's words, but they don't put them into practice; their hearts chase money and they speak deceitfully. Listening to God's word without obeying it is empty.
entries.33:32: To them Ezekiel is like a beautiful love song performed by a skilled musician—pleasant to hear but not taken to heart. People can enjoy hearing God's word while never letting it change them.
entries.33:33: When the predicted destruction actually happens, the people will know a real prophet was among them. The truth of God's word is proven when it comes to pass.
entries.34:1: God's message came to Ezekiel. This reminds us that what follows is not Ezekiel's own opinion but something God wanted said.
entries.34:2: God tells Ezekiel to speak against the leaders of Israel, pictured as shepherds. They were feeding themselves instead of caring for the people, and God says shepherds should feed the sheep, not themselves.
entries.34:3: The leaders took everything good from the people—milk, wool, meat—but gave nothing back. It means leaders who use people for their own benefit while ignoring their needs are doing wrong.
entries.34:4: The leaders failed to help the weak, sick, injured, lost, or straying, and were harsh with the strong. God notices when those in charge neglect the vulnerable and bully the rest.
entries.34:5: Because no one was truly caring for them, the people scattered and were easy prey. When leaders abandon their responsibility, ordinary people suffer and get hurt.
entries.34:6: God's people wandered everywhere with no one looking for them. God sees when people are lost and no one cares enough to go after them.
entries.34:7: God now turns to address the leaders directly. They need to listen carefully because God is about to hold them accountable.
entries.34:8: God swears by his own life that his people were scattered and harmed because the leaders fed themselves instead of the flock. God takes personally the harm done to people he calls his own.
entries.34:9: God repeats the call for the leaders to listen. This repetition shows how serious he is about their failure.
entries.34:10: God says he is against these leaders and will remove them from their position. He will rescue his people from leaders who treated them as food for themselves.
entries.34:11: God himself will step in and search for his scattered sheep. When human leaders fail, God does not abandon his people—he goes looking for them himself.
entries.34:12: Like a shepherd searching for lost sheep on a dark, cloudy day, God will rescue his people from everywhere they were scattered. No place is too far for God to find you.
entries.34:13: God will bring his people back from other nations to their own land and provide for them there. God's rescue includes bringing people home and giving them what they need.
entries.34:14: God promises good pasture and safe resting places on the mountains of Israel. He wants his people fed well and able to rest securely.
entries.34:15: God says plainly that he himself will feed his flock and give them rest. The care the leaders failed to give, God will give personally.
entries.34:16: God will search for the lost, bring back the strayed, bandage the broken, and strengthen the sick, but he will judge the fat and strong who abused others. God cares for the weak and holds the powerful accountable.
entries.34:17: God says he will judge between one sheep and another, including the rams and goats. God sees differences among his people and will settle who has treated whom unfairly.
entries.34:18: The strong sheep eat the good grass and then trample the rest, and muddy the clear water after drinking. It means some people take more than they need and spoil what others depend on.
entries.34:19: The weaker sheep are left eating trampled grass and drinking dirty water. God notices when the careless actions of some make life harder for others.
entries.34:20: God declares he will judge between the fat sheep and the thin sheep. He is not neutral when the strong take advantage of the weak.
entries.34:21: The strong pushed with shoulder and horn and scattered the weak. God sees bullying among his people and will not ignore it.
entries.34:22: God will rescue his flock so they are no longer plundered, and he will judge fairly between sheep. God promises protection for those being pushed around.
entries.34:23: God will appoint one shepherd over them, his servant David, to feed and care for them. This points to a future leader from David's line who will care for God's people rightly.
