entries.34:24: God will be their God and David their ruler, and God himself has promised it. The people can count on both God's care and a faithful human leader.
entries.34:25: God will make a peace agreement with them and remove dangerous animals from the land. They will live safely even in wild places, because God guarantees their security.
entries.34:26: God will send rain at the right times, showers of blessing. His care includes ordinary, timely provision that makes life grow and flourish.
entries.34:27: Trees will bear fruit and the land will produce crops, and the people will be safe. They will know God is real when he breaks their slavery and sets them free.
entries.34:28: Other nations will no longer take their goods, and wild animals will not harm them. They will live without fear, and no one will terrify them.
entries.34:29: God will give them a place of peace where they are not starved or shamed by other nations. God's blessing includes dignity, not just survival.
entries.34:30: Then they will know that God is with them and that they are his people. God's care is meant to make his presence and his love unmistakable.
entries.34:31: God closes by saying they are his sheep and he is their God. This is a simple, warm picture of belonging: God claims them and promises to care for them.
entries.35:1: God spoke directly to the prophet Ezekiel, giving him a message to deliver. It reminds us that what follows is not Ezekiel's own opinion but words from God.
entries.35:2: God told Ezekiel to face Mount Seir, a region linked with Edom, and speak God's message against it. It shows God addresses nations that oppose his people, not just individuals.
entries.35:3: God declares he is personally against Mount Seir and will act against it, leaving it ruined and shocking to see. It means no enemy of God's people escapes his notice or his response.
entries.35:4: The towns of that region would be emptied and left desolate, and the people would then recognize God's power. It shows that judgment aims to make people see who God really is.
entries.35:5: The people of Seir hated Israel endlessly and handed them over to be killed when they were already suffering. It means God sees cruelty done to his people and holds those responsible accountable.
entries.35:6: Because they chose violence and bloodshed, violence would chase them down in return. It teaches that those who live by cruelty will eventually face the same treatment.
entries.35:7: God would turn Mount Seir into a shocking wasteland and cut off all travel in and out. It means a place that once thrived through movement and trade would become empty and isolated.
entries.35:8: Their mountains, valleys, and streams would be filled with people killed in battle. It pictures total devastation, showing that God's judgment would reach every part of the land.
entries.35:9: The ruin would last permanently and the towns would stay empty, and people would recognize God through it. It means God's verdict on this nation was final, not temporary.
entries.35:10: They claimed Israel and Judah as their own land to take over, ignoring that God himself was present there. It warns against assuming God's people are abandoned and grabbing what belongs to him.
entries.35:11: God would treat them the same way they treated Israel in their anger, envy, and hatred, and they would learn who he is through his judgment. It means God measures out to people the same treatment they gave others.
entries.35:12: God had heard every bitter word they spoke, claiming Israel's ruined mountains were theirs to take. It reminds us that God hears what we say about his people, even when we think no one is listening.
entries.35:13: They boasted and spoke arrogantly against God, and he heard every word. It means proud talk against God is never ignored, even when it seems to go unnoticed.
entries.35:14: Because they celebrated when God's land lay in ruins, the same ruin would come to them. It teaches that gloating over someone else's downfall invites trouble on yourself.
entries.35:15: Mount Seir and all Edom would become a wasteland, and then they would know the Lord. It means the same destruction they enjoyed seeing on others would fall on them, and God would be recognized through it.
entries.36:1: God tells Ezekiel to speak to the mountains of Israel as if they were listening, announcing that God's word is coming to the land itself. It reminds the reader that God addresses even the ruined places and has not forgotten them.
entries.36:2: Israel's enemies gloated that the abandoned land was now theirs to keep. It shows how God notices when others mock his people's downfall and treat their land as spoils.
entries.36:3: God tells Ezekiel to speak because the nations had rejoiced over Israel's shame and gossiped about them. The reader can see that God takes seriously the mockery and slander his people endure.
entries.36:4: God speaks to every part of the empty, plundered land—mountains, hills, streams, valleys, and deserted towns—that neighbors had shamed. It means no part of the damage is beyond God's attention.
entries.36:5: God says in his burning anger that the surrounding nations, especially Edom, took his land with gladness and contempt. It shows God's jealousy for his land and his anger at those who seized it out of spite.
entries.36:6: God tells Ezekiel to announce to the whole land that he speaks in anger because Israel had to endure the nations' insults. The reader learns that God feels the shame his people carry.
entries.36:7: God swears an oath that the surrounding nations will themselves bear the shame they dumped on Israel. It means God promises to reverse the humiliation, turning it back on those who caused it.
entries.36:8: God promises that the mountains of Israel will again produce branches and fruit for his people, who are about to return. It means restoration is coming soon, and the land will once more provide for them.
entries.36:9: God says he is on Israel's side and will turn toward them so the land can be plowed and planted again. It means God himself backs the recovery of what was ruined.
entries.36:10: God promises to multiply the people of Israel and repopulate the towns, rebuilding the ruins. It means the empty places will be filled with life again.
entries.36:11: God will increase people and animals on the land, making it more populated and prosperous than before. It means the comeback will be greater than the original, and everyone will know God did it.
entries.36:12: God says his people Israel will walk on the land and possess it, and it will no longer rob them of children. It means the land will be a safe inheritance rather than a place of loss.
entries.36:13: God addresses the accusation that the land itself destroys people and causes the nation to lose children. It shows God is answering a cruel rumor spread about the land.
entries.36:14: God promises the land will no longer kill people or cause the nation to lose children. It means the land's sad reputation will be reversed.
entries.36:15: God says Israel will no longer hear the nations' insults or be looked down on by other peoples. It means the days of public shame are ending.
entries.36:16: This line simply marks a transition, noting that God's word came to Ezekiel again. It signals that a new message is beginning.
entries.36:17: God recalls that when Israel lived in the land, their behavior and actions made it unclean, like something ritually polluted. It means their wrong conduct contaminated the very place they lived.
entries.36:18: God poured out his anger on them because of the blood they shed in the land and the idols that defiled it. It means their violence and idolatry brought real consequences.
entries.36:19: God scattered them among the nations and judged them fairly for how they had lived. It means their exile was a just result of their own choices.
entries.36:20: Wherever the exiles went, they dragged God's holy name through the mud, since people said these were the Lord's people who had been driven from his land. It means their failure made God look weak in the eyes of outsiders.
entries.36:21: God says he spared concern for his holy name, which Israel had dishonored wherever they went. It means God cares about his reputation and acts to protect it.
entries.36:22: God tells Israel plainly that he is acting for the sake of his holy name, not because they deserve it, since they had dishonored that name among the nations. It means God's rescue is based on his own honor, not their merit.
entries.36:23: God will show his great name to be holy again, which Israel had disgraced among the nations, and the nations will recognize him when he does it through Israel. It means God will clear his reputation by restoring his people in public view.
entries.36:24: God promises to bring Israel out of the nations, gather them from every country, and return them to their own land. It means a real homecoming is coming.
entries.36:25: God will wash his people with clean water, cleansing them from all their impurities and idols. It means God himself will deal with the moral dirt that stained them.
entries.36:26: God promises a new heart and a new spirit, replacing their hard, stone-like heart with a soft, living one. It means deep inner change is God's gift, not something they must produce alone.
entries.36:27: God will put his own Spirit in them so they will follow his rules and actually keep his commands. It means obedience becomes possible because God's Spirit empowers it.
entries.36:28: They will live in the land God gave their ancestors, and the covenant formula will hold: they will be his people and he will be their God. It means restored relationship, not just restored property.
entries.36:29: God will free them from all their uncleanness, and when he speaks, grain will grow and food will be plentiful. It means cleansing and provision go together as God's work.
entries.36:30: God will make trees and fields produce abundantly so Israel will no longer be shamed among the nations for lack of food. It means the old humiliation of famine will be replaced with plenty.
entries.36:31: When they remember their evil ways and wrongdoings, they will hate themselves for their disgusting deeds. It means real repentance includes grief over the past, not excuses.
entries.36:32: God repeats that he is not doing this because they deserve it, and tells them to be ashamed and humbled over their ways. It means God's grace should produce humility, not pride.
entries.36:33: On the day God cleanses them from all their wrongdoing, he will repopulate the towns and rebuild the ruins. It means forgiveness and restoration are joined together.
entries.36:34: The land that was desolate will be farmed again instead of lying waste in the eyes of passersby. It means the visible ruin will become visible productivity.
entries.36:35: People will say the wasteland has become like the garden of Eden, and the ruined, empty towns are now walled and full of people. It means the transformation will be so dramatic that onlookers will talk about it.
entries.36:36: The surrounding nations will know that the Lord rebuilt what was torn down and replanted what was waste, and God guarantees he will do it. It means God's reputation is tied to finishing what he promises.
entries.36:37: God says Israel will again pray to him for this, and he will multiply them like a flock. It means God invites his people to ask for the very thing he has promised.
entries.36:38: The empty towns will be filled with people like the flocks brought to Jerusalem for the feasts, and everyone will know the Lord did it. It means the final picture is crowded, joyful abundance that points back to God.
entries.37:1: God's Spirit carried Ezekiel to a valley filled with bones. It means God can show us situations that look completely hopeless, and he is the one who leads us there.
entries.37:2: Ezekiel walked around and saw a huge number of bones that were completely dried out. It pictures something so dead and gone that no one would expect it to live again.
entries.37:3: God asked Ezekiel if these bones could live, and Ezekiel wisely said only God knows. It teaches us to admit we don't have the answer and to trust God with impossible situations.
entries.37:4: God told Ezekiel to speak his word to the dry bones. It shows that God's word is powerful enough to speak life into what seems dead.
entries.37:5: God promised to put breath into the bones so they would come alive. It means God himself gives life where there is none.
entries.37:6: God said he would rebuild the bodies and give them breath, and then they would know him. It means God's restoring work is meant to help people recognize who he is.
entries.37:7: Ezekiel obeyed and spoke, and the bones began rattling and joining together. It shows that when we simply do what God says, he does the miraculous part.
entries.37:8: The bodies formed with flesh and skin, but there was still no breath in them. It reminds us that having shape and structure isn't the same as having real life from God.
entries.37:9: God told Ezekiel to call the wind to breathe on the dead bodies. It shows that only God's Spirit can turn a lifeless thing into something truly alive.
entries.37:10: The breath came, the bodies came to life and stood up as a huge army. It pictures how God can turn a hopeless ruin into a strong, living people.
entries.37:11: God explained the bones were Israel, who felt their hope was gone and they were cut off. It shows God sees and understands when his people feel completely finished.
entries.37:12: God promised to open their graves and bring them back to their own land. It means God can bring his people out of the deepest place of despair.
entries.37:13: God said that when he raised them from their graves, they would know he is the Lord. It means God's rescue is designed to make people truly know him.
entries.37:14: God promised to put his Spirit in them so they could live and rest in their land. It means real life and peace come from God's Spirit within us.
entries.37:15: God began speaking to Ezekiel again with a new message. It shows God keeps guiding his people step by step.
entries.37:16: God told Ezekiel to write on one stick for Judah and another for Joseph's tribes. It was a visual way of showing two divided groups.
entries.37:17: God told Ezekiel to join the two sticks into one in his hand. It pictured God bringing divided people back together as one.
entries.37:18: God expected the people to ask what the sticks meant. It shows God welcomes honest questions about what he is doing.
entries.37:19: God said he would join Joseph's stick to Judah's so they became one in his hand. It means God himself is the one who unites people who were split apart.
entries.37:20: Ezekiel was to hold the joined sticks where everyone could see them. It means God's promises are meant to be shown openly, not kept hidden.
entries.37:21: God promised to gather the Israelites from the nations and bring them home. It means no distance or scattering is too far for God to bring his people back.
entries.37:22: God said they would become one nation under one king, never split again. It means God's plan is unity and lasting togetherness for his people.
entries.37:23: God promised to cleanse them from their idols and sins and be their God. It means God doesn't just rescue people; he also changes them from the inside.
entries.37:24: God said his servant David would be their king and they would follow his rules. It points to a good shepherd-king who leads people to obey God.
entries.37:25: God promised they would live in the land for generations with David as ruler forever. It means God's care for his people is meant to last, not fade away.
entries.37:26: God promised a lasting peace agreement, blessing, growth, and his holy place among them. It means God's presence with his people is the heart of his promise.
entries.37:27: God said his house would be over them and he would be their God. It means God wants to live close to his people and belong to them.
entries.37:28: The nations would recognize the Lord when his holy place was among Israel forever. It means God's presence with his people is a sign to the world of who he is.
entries.38:1: God speaks directly to the prophet Ezekiel, giving him a message to pass on. It reminds the reader that what follows is presented as God's own word, not Ezekiel's opinion.
entries.38:2: God tells Ezekiel to set his face against Gog, a powerful leader from the land of Magog and over several peoples, and to speak God's message against him. The reader sees that God takes a stand against this enemy and has a prophet announce it.
entries.38:3: God says plainly that he is against Gog, the ruler over those northern peoples. It means the reader can be sure this powerful leader is not beyond God's reach.
entries.38:4: God says he will turn Gog around and drag him out to war with his whole army, fully armed and huge. The point is that even this mighty force is under God's control, moved where he decides.
entries.38:5: Gog's army includes soldiers from Persia, Cush, and Put, all equipped with armor and helmets. It shows how large and well-prepared the opposing force is, yet still under God's authority.
entries.38:6: More peoples from the far north join Gog with their armies, making a vast coalition. The reader sees that the threat is enormous, but God has already named it and is not surprised.
entries.38:7: God tells Gog to get ready and prepare his forces for his orders. It means the enemy may prepare, but he will only act when God allows it.
entries.38:8: After a long time, Gog will be called to attack a land that has been restored to a gathered people living safely. The reader sees that God's people have been brought back and are at rest before this threat comes.
entries.38:9: Gog will sweep in like a storm or a cloud covering the whole land with his many forces. It pictures an overwhelming invasion that the reader can picture clearly.
entries.38:10: God says that on that day Gog will hatch an evil plan in his own mind. It shows the attack comes from Gog's own wicked intentions, not from God's character.
entries.38:11: Gog plans to attack quiet towns whose people live without walls, locks, or gates, feeling safe. The reader sees the enemy targeting the vulnerable and peaceful.
entries.38:12: Gog's aim is to seize property and goods from restored, prosperous people living in the center of the earth. It shows the attack is driven by greed for wealth.
entries.38:13: Trading peoples like Sheba, Dedan, and Tarshish ask Gog if he has come to plunder and carry off silver, gold, cattle, and goods. It shows even other nations recognize his motive as robbery.
entries.38:14: God tells Ezekiel to prophesy that when his people Israel live safely, Gog will certainly stir himself against them. The reader sees the attack is aimed at God's people precisely when they feel secure.
entries.38:15: Gog will come from his far northern home with a great army of horsemen and many peoples. It emphasizes the size and strength of the force coming against Israel.
entries.38:16: Gog will cover the land like a cloud and attack God's people in the last days, but God will use it to show the nations who he is. The reader learns that even an attack on God's people ends up displaying God's holiness.
entries.38:17: God reminds Gog that Israel's prophets long foretold this attack year after year. It shows this event was not a surprise but part of what God had already announced.
entries.38:18: When Gog attacks Israel, God's anger and fierce wrath will rise up. The reader sees that God takes the attack on his people personally and will respond.
entries.38:19: In his burning anger God declares there will be a great earthquake in the land of Israel. It signals that God himself will act powerfully against the invader.
entries.38:20: Everything on earth will tremble before God, mountains will fall, and every wall will collapse. The reader sees that no human defense or stronghold can stand when God acts.
entries.38:21: God will call for a sword against Gog throughout his mountains, and the soldiers will turn on each other. It shows God defeating the enemy partly by turning their own violence against themselves.
entries.38:22: God will judge Gog with disease, bloodshed, flooding rain, hail, fire, and burning sulfur on him and his armies. The reader sees God's full judgment falling on the attacker.
entries.38:23: God will show his greatness and holiness and make himself known to many nations, who will recognize that he is the Lord. The outcome is that people everywhere come to know who God is.
entries.39:1: God tells the prophet Ezekiel to speak directly against Gog, a powerful enemy leader, and to announce that God himself is opposed to him. For the reader, it means no enemy is beyond God's notice or power.
entries.39:2: God says he will turn this enemy around and pull him down from the far north to attack the mountains of Israel. It means God is in control even of the movements of those who oppose him.
entries.39:3: God will strike the enemy's weapons from his hands so his bow and arrows are useless. For the reader, it shows that human strength and weapons fail when God acts against them.
entries.39:4: The enemy army will fall on Israel's mountains and become food for birds and wild animals. It means defeat will be total and humiliating, with no army left standing.
entries.39:5: The enemy will fall in open country because God has declared it will happen. For the reader, God's word is certain and will not fail.
entries.39:6: God will send fire on Gog's land and on distant coastlands that feel safe. It means no place is too far or too secure to escape God's judgment.
entries.39:7: God will defend his holy name among his people Israel and stop it from being dishonored. The nations will then know that he alone is the holy God of Israel.
entries.39:8: God declares that this day is certain and will surely come, just as he promised. For the reader, it is a reminder that God's warnings are not empty threats.
entries.39:9: The people of Israel's towns will gather the enemy's abandoned weapons and burn them as firewood for seven years. It means the leftovers of war will supply their needs for a long time.
entries.39:10: They won't need to cut wood from fields or forests because the weapons will fuel their fires, and they will take back what was taken from them. It means God turns the enemy's threat into blessing for his people.
entries.39:11: God will give Gog a burial place in a valley east of the sea, and it will be named after Gog's vast crowd. It means the enemy's end will be marked and remembered.
entries.39:12: Israel will spend seven months burying the dead to make the land clean again. It means the aftermath of judgment is serious and requires real cleansing.
entries.39:13: All the people will help bury the dead, and this will bring them honor when God's glory is revealed. It means participating in God's work brings honor to his people.
entries.39:14: Men will be assigned to search the land and bury any remaining bodies after the seven months. It means cleansing is thorough and no part of the past is left to pollute the future.
entries.39:15: Anyone who finds a bone will mark the spot so the burial workers can bury it in the valley of Gog's crowd. It means even small remains are dealt with carefully.
entries.39:16: The whole army of Gog will be buried there, and so the land will be made clean. It means God's victory is complete and his land is restored.
entries.39:17: God calls the birds and wild animals to come to a great feast on the mountains of Israel, where they will eat flesh and drink blood. It pictures the enemy's defeat as a meal God himself prepares.
entries.39:18: The animals will eat the flesh of soldiers and drink the blood of princes, described like fat sheep, goats, and oxen. It means even the mightiest leaders will fall like sacrificial animals.
entries.39:19: The birds and beasts will eat and drink until they are full and overcome. It emphasizes how complete and overwhelming the defeat will be.
entries.39:20: At God's table the animals will feast on horses, chariots, and all the warriors. It means God's victory includes every level of the enemy's strength.
entries.39:21: God will display his glory among the nations, and they will see his judgment and his hand on his enemies. For the reader, God's actions are meant to be seen and known by all.
entries.39:22: From that day on, Israel will know for certain that the Lord is their God. It means God's rescue builds lasting trust in him.
entries.39:23: The nations will understand that Israel was taken captive because of their own sin, when God turned away from them and let their enemies defeat them. It means suffering was not random but tied to their wrongdoing.
entries.39:24: God treated Israel according to their unclean ways and sins and hid his face from them. It means sin has real consequences, including feeling cut off from God.
entries.39:25: God now promises to restore Jacob's fortunes, show mercy to all Israel, and defend the honor of his holy name. It means judgment is not the end of the story; God's mercy follows.
entries.39:26: When they live safely in their land with no one to frighten them, they will feel ashamed of all the wrong they did against God. It means safety and peace open the heart to honest repentance.
entries.39:27: God will bring them back from the nations and show himself holy among them in front of many peoples. It means God's rescue of his people displays his character to the world.
entries.39:28: They will know the Lord their God because he scattered them among the nations and then gathered them all back to their land, leaving none behind. It means God keeps his promises to the very end.
entries.39:29: God will no longer hide his face from them because he has poured out his Spirit on Israel. It means God's presence and Spirit restore the relationship that sin had broken.
entries.40:1: This dates the vision precisely: twenty-five years into the exile and fourteen years after Jerusalem fell. It tells the reader that God still speaks to his people long after disaster, on a specific, real day.
entries.40:2: In the vision God carries Ezekiel to a high mountain in Israel and shows him something like a city built opposite him. It means God is giving his exiled prophet a picture of restoration, not just words of comfort.
entries.40:3: Ezekiel sees a man who looks like polished bronze, holding a measuring cord and rod, standing in a gateway. The reader should picture God sending an expert to survey and explain the new structure.
entries.40:4: The man tells Ezekiel to look, listen, and take it all to heart, because he was brought there to see it and must later report it to Israel. It means pay close attention, because what God shows you is meant to be passed on.
entries.40:5: A wall surrounds the whole house, and the man measures it with a rod about ten feet long. It shows the whole structure is carefully planned and bounded, not vague or random.
entries.40:6: The man goes to the east gateway, climbs its steps, and measures the threshold. It means the tour starts at the entrance, the place where people would come in.
entries.40:7: The small guard rooms along the gateway are each one rod square, with five cubits between them, and the inner threshold is one rod. It shows the design is orderly and exact down to the smallest room.
entries.40:8: The man measures the covered passage of the gateway on its inner side. It means even the walkway inside the entrance is part of the carefully measured plan.
entries.40:9: The covered passage is eight cubits, with posts two cubits thick, and it faces inward. It shows the entrance has depth and structure, not just an opening in a wall.
entries.40:10: There are three guard rooms on each side of the east gateway, all the same size, with matching posts. It means the design is symmetrical and balanced, the same on both sides.
entries.40:11: The man measures the gateway opening as ten cubits wide and the passage as thirteen cubits. It shows the entrance is wide enough for crowds to pass through.
entries.40:12: A low barrier of one cubit stands in front of the rooms, and the rooms themselves are six cubits square. It means the space is laid out with care, with clear boundaries.
entries.40:13: He measures from the back of one room to the back of the opposite room, twenty-five cubits across. It shows the gateway's full width is exact and consistent.
entries.40:14: The covered way measures twenty cubits, and it opens onto the courtyard all around. It means the entrance connects to the wider space in a planned way.
entries.40:15: From the outer opening of the gateway to the front of its inner passage is fifty cubits. It shows the entrance is long and substantial, not a quick doorway.
entries.40:16: The rooms and posts have narrow, sloping windows all around, and palm trees are carved on the posts. It means the place is full of light and decorated with symbols of life and blessing.
entries.40:17: The man brings Ezekiel into the outer courtyard, which has a stone pavement and thirty rooms around it. It shows the temple area is a busy, structured place with space for many people.
entries.40:18: The stone pavement runs alongside the gateways and matches their length, forming the lower level. It means the courtyard's layout is tied directly to the entrances.
entries.40:19: He measures the courtyard from the lower gateway to the inner gateway as one hundred cubits, then turns north. It shows the space is large and measured precisely, and the tour continues.
entries.40:20: Ezekiel is shown the north gateway of the outer courtyard and it is measured too. It means every side of the building gets the same careful attention.
entries.40:21: The north gateway has three rooms on each side, with posts and passages the same size as the first gateway, fifty by twenty-five cubits. It shows the design is consistent from gate to gate.
entries.40:22: Its windows, passages, and palm trees match the east gateway, and seven steps lead up to it. It means the north entrance is a copy of the first, keeping the whole building uniform.
entries.40:23: A gateway to the inner courtyard faces the north gateway, and the distance between them is one hundred cubits. It shows the inner and outer courts line up exactly, like the east side.
entries.40:24: The man takes Ezekiel south, where another gateway faces south, and measures its rooms, posts, and passages. It means the south side is surveyed just like the others.
entries.40:25: This gateway has windows all around like the others and measures fifty by twenty-five cubits. It shows the south entrance matches the rest of the building.
entries.40:26: Seven steps lead up to it, its passage faces inward, and palm trees are carved on its posts on both sides. It means the south gateway shares the same steps and decorations as the others.
entries.40:27: A gateway to the inner courtyard faces south, and the distance between the two south gateways is one hundred cubits. It shows the south side is laid out exactly like the east and north.
entries.40:28: The man brings Ezekiel into the inner courtyard through the south gateway and measures it the same way. It means the inner court is checked with the same standard as the outer.
entries.40:29: Its rooms, posts, and passages are measured by the same standard as before. It shows the inner court follows the same careful pattern.
entries.40:30: This gateway has windows all around and measures fifty by twenty-five cubits. It means the inner south gateway is the same size as the outer ones.
entries.40:31: Its passage faces the outer courtyard, palm trees are on its posts, and eight steps lead up to it. It means this inner gateway is slightly taller in steps but still matches the pattern.
entries.40:32: The man brings Ezekiel into the inner courtyard on the east side and measures that gateway too. It means the east inner entrance is surveyed like the south one.
entries.40:33: Its rooms, posts, and passages match the same measurements, with windows all around, fifty by twenty-five cubits. It shows the inner east gateway is built to the same standard.
entries.40:34: Its passage faces the outer courtyard, palm trees are on its posts on both sides, and eight steps lead up. It means this gateway shares the same design as the inner south gateway.
entries.40:35: The man brings Ezekiel to the north gateway and measures it by the same standard. It means the last side of the inner court is checked like all the others.
entries.40:36: Its rooms, posts, and passage have the same measurements, with windows all around, fifty by twenty-five cubits. It shows the inner north gateway matches the rest exactly.
entries.40:37: Its posts face the outer courtyard, palm trees are on the posts on both sides, and eight steps lead up. It means this gateway is identical in design to the other inner gateways.
entries.40:38: A room with a door in the gateway passage is where the burnt offerings are washed. It means the building includes practical space for preparing sacrifices.
entries.40:39: In the gateway passage there are two tables on each side where the burnt offering, sin offering, and guilt offering are killed. It shows the place is set up for the serious work of sacrifice.
entries.40:40: On the outer side, north of the steps up to the gateway, there are two more tables. It means there is ample space for the work of offering, arranged in an orderly way.
entries.40:41: This describes eight tables in the temple area where animals for sacrifices were killed. It shows the careful, orderly way God planned worship for his people.
entries.40:42: Four stone tables were set aside for the burnt offerings, with the tools for preparing the animals placed on them. The detail shows that even the practical parts of worship were planned with care.
entries.40:43: The tables had a raised rim about a hand-width wide, and the meat of the offerings was laid on them. This reminds the reader that worship involved real, physical preparation, not just words.
entries.40:44: The guide brought Ezekiel into the inner courtyard, where two rooms faced opposite directions near the north and south gateways. These rooms were part of the temple's ordered layout.
entries.40:45: The room facing south was for the priests responsible for looking after the temple building itself. Different priests had different duties in keeping the temple running.
entries.40:46: The room facing north was for the priests who served at the altar, specifically the descendants of Zadok, who were allowed to come closest to the Lord. It shows that drawing near to God was a serious privilege given to particular people.
entries.40:47: The open courtyard was measured as a perfect square, a hundred cubits on each side, with the altar standing in front of the temple. The symmetry and the central altar show that worship of God was the heart of the whole design.
entries.40:48: Ezekiel was led to the entrance porch of the temple, and its pillars and doorway were measured. The precise measurements show that this was a real, carefully built structure, not a vague vision.
entries.40:49: The entrance porch was twenty cubits long and twelve wide, reached by ten steps, with a pillar on each side. The steps and pillars gave the entrance a sense of dignity and made clear that approaching God's house was a deliberate, upward journey.
entries.41:1: God's guide measured the temple's entrance walls, showing that even the doorway into God's house is carefully planned. For the reader, it suggests that coming near to God is something to take seriously.
entries.41:2: The guide measured the wide entrance and the main room beyond it, noting its length and width. This tells the reader that the place of worship was large and orderly, made to hold God's people.
entries.41:3: The guide went further in and measured a narrower inner doorway leading deeper into the temple. It reminds the reader that drawing closer to God's most sacred space meant passing through a smaller, more careful entrance.
entries.41:4: The innermost room was a perfect square, and the guide called it the most holy place. For the reader, this marks the heart of the temple, the spot set apart as closest to God's presence.
entries.41:5: The guide measured the temple's outer wall and the small rooms built around it. This shows the reader that the temple was a solid, well-built structure with space around it for service.
entries.41:6: Three levels of small rooms were stacked around the temple, held up by ledges set into its wall. It pictures a carefully designed building where every part has its place and support.
entries.41:7: The higher the side rooms went, the wider they became, and stairs connected the floors. For the reader, it suggests that moving upward in God's house means growing room and orderly progress.
entries.41:8: The guide noticed a raised stone platform all around the temple, giving the side rooms a tall, firm base. It shows the reader that God's house rests on a solid foundation.
entries.41:9: A thick outer wall surrounded the side rooms, with open space left between them and the temple. This tells the reader that the design kept clear, orderly space around what was holy.
entries.41:10: A wide open area ran all the way around the temple. For the reader, it pictures room set aside around God's house, keeping it distinct from everything else.
entries.41:11: The open space had doorways on the north and south leading out from the side rooms. It shows the reader that the temple's design provided clear ways in and out for those who served there.
entries.41:12: A large separate building stood on the west side, measured with its own thick walls. This tells the reader that the whole temple complex, not just the main room, was planned and measured out.
entries.41:13: The main temple and the separate area with its building each measured a hundred cubits long. For the reader, it shows the whole sacred site was laid out on a grand, consistent scale.
entries.41:14: The front of the temple facing east, along with the separate area, was a hundred cubits wide. It reminds the reader that the entrance side of God's house was broad and open.
entries.41:15: The guide measured the rear building and the pillared walkways on both sides, all a hundred cubits long. This shows the reader that the temple was surrounded by covered walkways, giving shelter and order.
entries.41:16: The temple had angled windows and covered walkways, with wood paneling from the floor up to the windows. For the reader, it pictures a carefully finished house of worship, full of light and craft.
entries.41:17: The woodwork continued over the doorway and along the walls, inside and out. It tells the reader that no part of the temple was left unfinished or plain.
entries.41:18: The walls were carved with winged beings and palm trees, a palm tree between each pair of winged ones. For the reader, it shows God's house decorated with pictures of his heavenly servants and life.
entries.41:19: Each carved winged being had a human face turned one way and a lion's face the other. This tells the reader that the temple's art pictured both human and strong, wild life in God's presence.
entries.41:20: From the floor up to the windows, the walls were covered with these carved winged beings and palm trees. It shows the reader that the whole inside of the temple was filled with these sacred pictures.
entries.41:21: This verse describes the doorposts of the temple being square, and it notes that the front of the sanctuary looked like something made of wood. For the reader, it's a reminder that the temple was built with careful, orderly design as a place set apart for worship.
entries.41:22: A wooden altar stood there, and the guide called it the table before the Lord. For the reader, it pictures a simple wooden table set apart for worship in God's presence.
entries.41:23: The temple had two doors. This tells the reader that entry into God's house was through a pair of doors, a deliberate and formal way in.
entries.41:24: Each door had two leaves that folded open, two for one door and two for the other. It shows the reader that the temple's doors were made to open wide for those who came to worship.
entries.41:25: The doors were carved with the same winged beings and palm trees as the walls, and a wooden frame stood outside the covered way. For the reader, it shows the temple's beauty carried right through to its entrances.
entries.41:26: Sloping windows and palm tree carvings decorated the sides of the covered walkway and the side rooms. It tells the reader that even the outer parts of the temple were finished with care and beauty.
entries.42:1: A guide leads the prophet out to the north side of the temple area to show him a set of rooms. This shows God carefully laying out the spaces connected to worship.
entries.42:2: These north-side rooms measured a hundred cubits long and fifty wide. The exact measurements show that this temple plan is ordered and deliberate, not vague.
entries.42:3: The rooms stood across from a twenty-cubit strip of the inner courtyard and the stone pavement of the outer courtyard, with balconies facing each other on the third level. The design is detailed and symmetrical, showing careful planning.
entries.42:4: A walkway ten cubits wide and a hundred long ran in front of the rooms, with doors opening to the north. The rooms were easy to reach, arranged for practical use.
entries.42:5: The upper rooms were smaller because the balconies took up more of their space than on the lower floors. Even small details of the building are worked out in the vision.
entries.42:6: The rooms were built on three levels without the kind of pillars the outer courtyard had, so the top floor was narrower than the ones below. The structure was solid and self-supporting, built to last.
entries.42:7: An outer wall ran alongside the rooms toward the outer courtyard and was fifty cubits long. This wall marked the boundary of the rooms' area.
entries.42:8: The rooms facing the outer courtyard were fifty cubits long, while the space in front of the temple was a hundred cubits. The different lengths show the careful layout of the whole complex.
entries.42:9: A stairway or entrance at the east end led up into these rooms from the outer courtyard. There was a clear, set way in for those who used them.
entries.42:10: The prophet is also shown rooms on the south side, in front of the separate area and the building. The same arrangement appears on both sides, keeping the design balanced.
entries.42:11: The south rooms had a walkway just like the north ones, with the same length, width, exits, and doors. Both sides were built to the same pattern.
entries.42:12: A door on the south side opened toward the east at the head of the outer wall, giving access from the courtyard. Entry was provided in an orderly way.
entries.42:13: The guide explains that these north and south rooms are holy, where priests eat the most holy offerings and store the grain, sin, and guilt offerings. This shows that what belongs to God is kept separate and treated with respect.
entries.42:14: Priests must change out of their holy robes before going out to the people, leaving them in the holy rooms. Ordinary life and holy service are kept distinct, reminding readers that approaching God is serious.
entries.42:15: After measuring the inside of the temple, the guide brings the prophet out through the east gate and measures the whole area around it. The vision ends with a full survey of the entire site.
entries.42:16: He measured the east side at five hundred cubits with the measuring rod. The whole boundary is being marked out precisely.
entries.42:17: He measured the north side at five hundred cubits as well. Each side matches, showing a perfect square.
entries.42:18: He measured the south side at five hundred cubits. The same measurement on every side shows complete order.
entries.42:19: He measured the west side at five hundred cubits too. All four sides are equal, completing the square.
entries.42:20: The whole area was a square five hundred cubits on each side, with a wall all around to separate the holy from the common. God's holy space is clearly marked off from ordinary life, teaching the reader that holiness matters.
entries.43:1: God shows Ezekiel a gateway facing east, setting up what comes next. For the reader, it signals that God is about to return to his house from a specific direction.
entries.43:2: God's glory comes back from the east with a sound like rushing water, and the whole earth shines with it. It means God's presence is powerful and unmistakable, and he is returning to his people.
entries.43:3: Ezekiel recognizes this glory as the same he saw in earlier visions, and he falls face down in awe. It shows that God is consistent, and that meeting him rightly humbles us.
entries.43:4: The Lord's glory enters the temple through the east gate. It means God is actually taking up residence in his house again, not just visiting.
entries.43:5: The Spirit lifts Ezekiel into the inner court, and he sees the whole house filled with God's glory. It means God's presence fills everything, and the reader is invited to see that his glory is not partial.
entries.43:6: A voice speaks from inside the house while the man stands beside Ezekiel. It means God himself is speaking, giving the explanation of what Ezekiel sees.
entries.43:7: God says this is his throne and footstool, where he will live among Israel forever, and they must stop defiling his name. It means God wants a permanent home with his people, and their loyalty to him matters.
entries.43:8: Israel had built their doorways right next to God's, mixing their idolatry with his worship, so he punished them. It means God will not share his place with rival loyalties, and careless closeness to sin brings judgment.
entries.43:9: God calls the people to put away their sinful ways and their dead kings far from him, and then he will live among them forever. It means repentance is the path to lasting fellowship with God.
entries.43:10: God tells Ezekiel to describe the house to Israel so they will feel shame for their sin and pay attention to the design. It means seeing God's standards should make us honest about our failures.
entries.43:11: If they are ashamed, Ezekiel is to teach them the house's structure, exits, and rules so they can obey them. It means real shame leads to learning God's ways and actually doing them.
entries.43:12: The law of the house is that the whole area on top of the mountain is most holy. It means God's dwelling place is set apart entirely for him, and holiness is its defining mark.
entries.43:13: Ezekiel is given the altar's measurements, using a standard cubit plus a handbreadth. It means God cares about exact details in worship, and the reader sees that approaching him is not casual.
entries.43:14: The altar's base and shelves are measured in steps of height and width. It means the altar is built in ordered stages, showing that worship has a structure God defines.
entries.43:15: The fireplace is four cubits high with horns rising a cubit from it. It means the altar is a real place of sacrifice, and the horns mark it as a place of atonement and appeal.
entries.43:16: The fireplace is a square, twelve cubits by twelve. It means the altar is balanced and complete in its proportions, reflecting God's order in worship.
entries.43:17: The shelf is fourteen cubits square with a half-cubit rim and a one-cubit base, and steps face east. It means the altar is carefully arranged, and the east-facing steps connect with God's glory coming from the east.
entries.43:18: God gives rules for the altar: burnt offerings are made on it and blood is drained out. It means sacrifice and blood are central to how this altar is used, pointing to atonement.
entries.43:19: The Zadokite priests who come near to serve God are given a young ox for a sin offering. It means God appoints who may approach him, and sin must be dealt with first.
entries.43:20: Some of the ox's blood is put on the altar's horns, corners, and rim to cleanse it and make it free from sin. It means the altar itself needs purification, showing how seriously God treats sin.
entries.43:21: The sin-offering ox is burned in the appointed place outside the holy area. It means sin is removed from the sacred space and dealt with where God directs.
entries.43:22: On the second day a flawless male goat is offered as a sin offering, and the altar is cleansed just as with the ox. It means cleansing is repeated and thorough, not a one-time gesture.
entries.43:23: After the cleansing, a flawless young ox and a flawless ram are offered. It means God requires offerings without defect, showing that he deserves the best and the whole.
entries.43:24: The animals are brought before the Lord, salted by the priests, and offered as a burnt offering. It means worship is presented to God in the way he prescribed, with salt marking purity and covenant.
entries.43:25: For seven days a goat is given as a sin offering, along with a young ox and a ram without defect. It means atonement is a sustained, complete process, not a quick fix.
entries.43:26: For seven days they make offerings to take away sin from the altar and make it clean and holy. It means the altar is set apart for God through repeated cleansing, showing holiness is serious.
entries.43:27: After those days, from the eighth day on, the priests offer burnt and peace offerings, and God says he will accept the people. It means once cleansing is complete, fellowship with God is restored and he takes pleasure in his people.
entries.44:1: The prophet is brought back to the east gate of the temple area and finds it closed. This signals that God is about to explain something special about this gate.
entries.44:2: God says this gate must stay shut because he himself entered through it, making it holy. Some places are set apart for God alone and are not for ordinary use.
entries.44:3: Only the ruler is allowed to sit in that gateway to eat his meal in God's presence, entering and leaving by a covered path. Even the leader has limited access and must approach God on God's terms.
entries.44:4: The prophet is led to the north gate and sees the Lord's glory filling the temple, and he falls face down in awe. God's presence is overwhelming and deserves deep reverence.
entries.44:5: God tells the prophet to pay close attention to everything about the temple's rules and its entrances and exits. We should listen carefully and take God's instructions to heart rather than treating them casually.
entries.44:6: God tells Israel to stop their disgusting practices, calling them stubborn and out of control. God's patience has limits, and he calls his people to turn from wrong behavior.
entries.44:7: Israel had let foreigners who were not committed to God enter the holy place and had defiled the offerings, breaking God's covenant. God takes it seriously when people treat holy things as ordinary.
entries.44:8: The people had failed to care for God's holy things and had put others in charge of his work. Neglecting our responsibilities toward God is itself a serious failure.
entries.44:9: God rules that no foreigner whose heart and body are not set apart for him may enter his holy place. Being part of God's people requires real commitment, not just being nearby.
entries.44:10: The Levites who wandered from God to follow idols will still bear the consequences of their unfaithfulness. Turning away from God has real costs, even for those who serve him.
entries.44:11: These Levites may still serve in the temple as guards and helpers who handle the offerings for the people. God in mercy gives them work, but not the full honor of the priesthood.
entries.44:12: Because they served the people in front of idols and led Israel into sin, God's judgment is against them. Leaders who cause others to sin face serious accountability.
entries.44:13: They will not come near God to serve as priests or touch his most holy things, and they will carry the shame of what they did. Lost privilege and shame are the result of unfaithfulness.
entries.44:14: God still assigns them responsibility for the general care and work of the temple. Even after failure, God gives people a place to serve, though perhaps a humbler one.
entries.44:15: The priests descended from Zadok stayed faithful when Israel turned away, so they alone may come near God to serve and offer sacrifices. God honors those who remain faithful to him.
entries.44:16: These faithful priests may enter the holy place and approach God's table to do his work and care for his house. Close access to God is a privilege given to those who stay loyal to him.
entries.44:17: When these priests enter the inner court, they must wear linen robes and no wool. God cares about the details of how his worship is carried out.
entries.44:18: They must wear linen head coverings and trousers and nothing that makes them sweat. God's service is to be done with dignity and care, not in a careless or uncomfortable way.
entries.44:19: When they go out to the people, they must change out of their priestly robes and leave them in the holy rooms so the people are not made holy by contact with them. Holiness must be handled carefully, keeping the sacred distinct from the ordinary.
entries.44:20: The priests must not shave their heads completely or let their hair grow long, but keep it neatly trimmed. God's servants should present themselves with order and self-control.
entries.44:21: Priests must not drink wine before entering the inner court. Those who serve God in holy places need clear minds and self-control.
entries.44:22: Priests may not marry a widow or a divorced woman, but only a virgin from Israel or the widow of a priest. God sets standards for the family life of those who serve him.
entries.44:23: The priests must teach the people the difference between what is holy and what is common, and between clean and unclean. Spiritual leaders are responsible for helping people understand God's standards.
entries.44:24: In disputes the priests act as judges according to God's decisions, and they must keep his laws, feasts, and Sabbaths. God's people are to be guided by his rules in both daily life and worship.
entries.44:25: Priests must not touch a dead body and become unclean, except for close family like a parent, child, or unmarried sister. God allows grief and family duty but still guards the holiness of his servants.
entries.44:26: After becoming clean again, the priest must wait seven days. Cleansing and restoration before God take time and are not to be rushed.
entries.44:27: On the day he returns to the inner court to serve, the priest must bring a sin offering. Even God's servants need forgiveness and cleansing before they approach him.
entries.44:28: The priests will have no land inheritance because God himself is their inheritance and property. God himself is the greatest possession and reward of those who serve him.
entries.44:29: The priests will live on the grain offerings, sin offerings, and guilt offerings, and on everything specially dedicated to the Lord in Israel. God provides for those who give their lives to his service.
entries.44:30: The best of the firstfruits and every special offering belongs to the priests, and giving the first of your bread brings blessing on your household. Honoring God first with what we have brings blessing.
entries.44:31: Priests may not eat any bird or animal that died on its own or was killed by another animal. God's servants are to avoid what is unclean even in small, everyday matters.
entries.45:1: When the land is divided, a special strip is to be set aside as the Lord's own holy portion, measured out at 25,000 by 20,000. This teaches the reader that God comes first, and part of what we receive is reserved for him.
entries.45:2: Inside that holy area, a square of 500 by 500 is for the sanctuary itself, with an open border of fifty cubits around it. It shows that the place of worship is to be kept separate and treated with respect.
entries.45:3: Within the holy portion, a strip 25,000 long and 10,000 wide is measured out, and the most holy place sits inside it. The reader learns that God's presence has a set, carefully ordered place at the center of his people's life.
entries.45:4: This holy land belongs to the priests who serve at the sanctuary and draw near to the Lord, and it provides their homes, pasture, and cattle. It means those who give their lives to God's service are to be cared for.
entries.45:5: A separate strip of the same length but 10,000 wide is set aside for the Levites who serve the temple, to be their own property with towns to live in. God makes sure his servants have a secure place to dwell.
entries.45:6: Next to the holy portion, a strip 5,000 wide and 25,000 long is set aside as property for the city, belonging to all the people of Israel. It shows that ordinary community life has its own God-given place alongside worship.
entries.45:7: The ruler gets land on both sides of the holy portion and the city property, stretching east and west along the same lines as the tribal portions. The leader is given a fair share without taking from anyone else's inheritance.
entries.45:8: This land is the ruler's inheritance in Israel, and the rulers must stop being harsh masters over the people and instead give each tribe its land. It means leaders are to use their position to serve and protect, not to exploit.
entries.45:9: The Lord tells the rulers of Israel to stop their violence and plundering, to do what is right and fair, and to stop driving his people off their land. It is a direct call for leaders to end injustice and treat people honestly.
entries.45:10: They are to use honest scales, honest dry measures, and honest liquid measures. It means fairness in buying and selling is a matter of obedience to God, not just good business.
entries.45:11: The dry and liquid measures are to match each other, both based on a tenth of a homer. The reader learns that consistent, reliable standards keep trade fair for everyone.
entries.45:12: The money system is fixed: twenty gerahs to a shekel, and fifty shekels to a maneh. Clear, standard weights and values protect people from being cheated.
entries.45:13: The offering to be given is a sixth of an ephah of wheat and a sixth of an ephah of barley out of each homer. It means giving to God is to be a regular, measured part of what we harvest.
entries.45:14: The oil offering is fixed at a tenth of a bath out of each cor, since ten baths make a cor. God's people are to give from their produce in a set, orderly way.
entries.45:15: One lamb is to be taken from every two hundred across the families of Israel, for offerings that deal with sin. It shows that atonement is provided for the whole community through a shared, modest cost.
entries.45:16: All the people are to bring this offering to the ruler. The whole community shares in providing what is needed for worship.
entries.45:17: The ruler is responsible for supplying the offerings at the feasts, new moons, and Sabbaths, including the sin offering for Israel. Leadership means bearing the cost of making sure worship and reconciliation with God happen.
entries.45:18: On the first day of the first month, a young ox without any defect is to be used to cleanse the holy place. It teaches that God's dwelling must be kept pure, and that cleansing is a regular need.
entries.45:19: The priest puts some of the sin offering's blood on the doorposts of the temple, the corners of the altar, and the doorway of the inner court. It shows that sin touches every part of the place of worship and needs to be dealt with thoroughly.
entries.45:20: The same cleansing is done on the seventh day of the month for anyone who sins by mistake or is weak, so the temple is made free from sin. It means God makes provision even for unintentional failures and for the vulnerable.
entries.45:21: On the fourteenth day of the first month, the people are to keep the Passover, a seven-day feast eating bread made without yeast. It recalls God's rescue of his people and calls them to remember it with humility.
entries.45:22: On that day the ruler offers an ox as a sin offering for himself and for all the people. It shows that leaders too need forgiveness, and that they stand with the people before God.
entries.45:23: During the seven days of the feast, the ruler gives seven oxen and seven sheep without defect each day as a burnt offering, plus a goat each day for sin. It means worship is to be generous, regular, and focused on dealing with sin.
entries.45:24: With each ox and each sheep, the ruler gives a set amount of grain and oil as a meal offering. The offerings are to be complete and properly matched, not careless or half-hearted.
entries.45:25: In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day, the same offerings are made for the seven-day feast: sin offering, burnt offering, grain offering, and oil. It shows God's people are to keep returning to him in worship at set times, with the same care each time.
entries.46:1: God says the east gate of the inner courtyard stays shut on the six working days but is opened on the Sabbath and at each new moon. For the reader, this shows that regular times of worship are set apart and matter to God.
entries.46:2: The ruler enters by the outer gateway and stands at the doorway while the priests offer his sacrifices, then he leaves and the gate stays open until evening. It means leaders are to worship humbly under God's rules, not on their own terms.
entries.46:3: Ordinary people gather at that doorway to worship the Lord on Sabbaths and new moons. It means worship is for everyone, not just leaders, and God expects his people to show up together.
entries.46:4: On the Sabbath the ruler brings six lambs and a ram, all without any defect. It means offerings to God were to be the best, with nothing flawed or second-rate.
entries.46:5: The grain offering is a set amount for the ram, as much as he can afford for the lambs, plus a set amount of oil. It means God's requirements are specific but also take a person's ability into account.
entries.46:6: At the new moon the ruler brings a young bull, six lambs, and a ram, all without defect. It means the monthly worship also called for generous, unblemished giving to God.
entries.46:7: The grain and oil offerings are measured out to match the bull and the ram, with the lambs given according to what he can afford. It means the offering is to fit the sacrifice and the giver's means.
entries.46:8: The ruler must enter and leave through the same covered gateway. It means order and consistency are expected in how leaders approach God.
entries.46:9: At the festivals, people who enter by the north gate must leave by the south gate, and vice versa, never turning back. It means worship is to be orderly and move forward, not chaotic or self-directed.
entries.46:10: The ruler goes in with the people and comes out with them. It means the leader is not above the congregation but worships alongside them.
entries.46:11: At festivals the grain offering is a set amount for the bull and the ram, with the lambs given as he is able, plus a set amount of oil. It means the same careful, generous standard applies at the big gatherings too.
entries.46:12: When the ruler freely gives a voluntary offering, the east gate is opened for him, and it is shut again after he leaves. It means God welcomes gifts given freely, but still within his ordered way.
entries.46:13: A one-year-old lamb without defect is to be offered to the Lord every morning. It means daily, faithful devotion matters, not just occasional big gestures.
entries.46:14: Each morning a grain offering of fine flour and oil is to accompany the lamb, as a lasting rule. It means worship is to be regular and consistent, day after day.
entries.46:15: The lamb, grain, and oil are to be offered every morning as a continual burnt offering. It means God's people are to keep showing up before him without fail.
entries.46:16: If the ruler gives property to one of his sons, it becomes the son's permanent inheritance. It means gifts meant for family are to be secure and not taken back.
entries.46:17: If the ruler gives property to a servant, it belongs to the servant only until the year of release, then it returns to the ruler's sons. It means temporary gifts stay temporary, and family inheritance is protected.
entries.46:18: The ruler must not seize people's property to give to his sons, so that no one is driven off their land. It means leaders must not use power to take what belongs to others, even for good-sounding reasons.
entries.46:19: The guide brings Ezekiel through a side entrance into the priests' holy rooms on the north side, and he sees a place at their west side. It means God's holy space is carefully arranged and set apart for those who serve him.
entries.46:20: This is where the priests cook the guilt offering, the sin offering, and the grain offering so they don't have to carry them into the outer court. It means holy things are handled with care and kept in their proper place.
entries.46:21: The guide takes Ezekiel out to the outer court and leads him around its four corners, where he sees enclosed spaces. It means the temple's design is complete and orderly on every side.
entries.46:22: In each of the four corners are walled-in areas, all the same size, forty cubits long and thirty wide. It means God's house is planned with precision and fairness, not left to chance.
entries.46:23: A low wall runs around the inside of each corner area, with cooking places built under it all around. It means practical work for worship is provided for and organized.
entries.46:24: The guide explains these are the kitchens where the temple servants cook the people's offerings. It means the everyday work of preparing worship is real service to God, not lesser work.
entries.47:1: A stream of water is flowing out from under the temple toward the east, past the altar. It shows that life and blessing come from God's presence, and it invites the reader to see God as the source of life.
entries.47:2: The man leads Ezekiel around to the outside east gate, where he sees the same water trickling out. Even small beginnings of God's work are worth noticing.
entries.47:3: The man measures about a thousand cubits and leads Ezekiel through water that only covers his feet. God's life-giving work starts small and grows step by step.
entries.47:4: After another thousand cubits the water reaches the knees, then the waist. The stream keeps getting deeper, showing that God's blessing grows the further you go with him.
entries.47:5: After another thousand cubits it is a deep river too strong to cross. What began as a trickle has become something only God could produce.
entries.47:6: The man asks Ezekiel whether he has really taken this in, then brings him to the riverbank. God wants us to stop and pay attention to what he is doing.
entries.47:7: Ezekiel sees many trees lining both banks of the river. Where God's life flows, abundance grows on every side.
entries.47:8: The man explains that the water flows east into the valley and down to the sea, and it turns the salty water fresh. God's presence brings healing even to dead places.
entries.47:9: Wherever the river goes, living creatures thrive and fish become plentiful. The river stands for God's life-giving power, which brings life wherever it reaches.
entries.47:10: Fishermen will line the shore from En-gedi to En-eglaim, and the catch will be as varied and plentiful as in the Great Sea. God's healing makes ordinary work fruitful again.
entries.47:11: The swampy places and pools stay salty and are left alone. Not everything is changed, which reminds the reader that God's renewal is his to give as he chooses.
entries.47:12: Trees along the river bear fruit every month and their leaves never wither, because the water comes from the holy place. God's presence gives lasting nourishment and healing to those who live near him.
entries.47:13: God sets the borders for how the land will be divided among the twelve tribes, with Joseph's family getting two shares. God keeps his promises to his people in an orderly way.
entries.47:14: The land is to be split evenly among the tribes, because God swore to give it to their ancestors. The reader can trust that God remembers the promises he made long ago.
entries.47:15: The northern border runs from the Great Sea toward Hethlon and on to the road to Hamath. God marks out real, specific places, not vague ideas.
entries.47:16: The border passes through Zedad, Berothah, and Sibraim, between Damascus and Hauran. These details show the land is a concrete gift with clear boundaries.
entries.47:17: The northern line runs from the sea to Hazar-enon, with Damascus and Hamath to the north. God defines exactly what belongs to his people.
entries.47:18: The eastern border runs between Hauran, Damascus, Gilead, and Israel, with the Jordan as the line down to the eastern sea. God's gift has limits he himself sets.
entries.47:19: The southern border goes from Tamar to the waters of Meribath-kadesh and on to the stream of Egypt and the Great Sea. Every side of the land is accounted for.
entries.47:20: The western border is the Great Sea, from the south up to a point opposite Hamath. The whole land is enclosed by God's careful design.
entries.47:21: God tells the people to divide the land among themselves tribe by tribe. Each family receives its own share of what God has given.
entries.47:22: Foreigners living among the Israelites who have children there must be treated like native-born Israelites and given land among the tribes. God's family includes outsiders who settle among his people.
entries.47:23: Wherever a foreigner lives, that tribe must give him his share of land. God insists that those who join his people are not left out.
entries.48:1: This starts a map of how the land will be split among Israel's tribes, beginning with Dan's share in the far north. It shows God giving each tribe a settled place in the restored land.
entries.48:2: Asher's share sits right next to Dan's, running across the land from east to west. Each tribe gets its own strip of ground, side by side.
entries.48:3: Naphtali's share comes next, also stretching from east to west. The tribes are arranged in an orderly way, each with a place.
entries.48:4: Manasseh's share lies next to Naphtali's, again running east to west. God's plan gives every tribe a clear, fair portion.
entries.48:5: Ephraim's share follows Manasseh's, east to west. The arrangement keeps going in order, tribe after tribe.
entries.48:6: Reuben's share comes next in the row, east to west. Each tribe's land is equal in this picture, showing fairness.
entries.48:7: Judah's share is the last of these northern strips, east to west. Judah's place is special because the holy area comes right next to it.
entries.48:8: Next to Judah is a special strip of land set apart as an offering to God, with the holy place at its center. This land is reserved for worship rather than for any tribe.
entries.48:9: This special offering to the Lord is a square area, measured out exactly. It is dedicated entirely to God.
entries.48:10: Within that holy area, the priests get a long strip of land, with the Lord's holy place in the middle. Those who serve God are given a place close to him.
entries.48:11: This land is for the priests from Zadok's family, who stayed faithful when others wandered away. God remembers and rewards those who stay loyal to him.
entries.48:12: Their portion is the most holy part of the land, set right next to the Levites' land. It is the best and most sacred share.
entries.48:13: The Levites get a strip of land next to the priests', measured out the same way. They too have a secure place in God's plan.
entries.48:14: This land must never be sold or traded away, because it belongs to the Lord. Some things are set apart for God and stay that way.
entries.48:15: The remaining strip of land is for ordinary use, for the city and its open land, with the town in the middle. Not everything is sacred space; there is room for everyday life too.
entries.48:16: The town itself is a square, with each side measuring the same. The city is laid out with order and care.
entries.48:17: Around the town is open land on every side, measured out evenly. The city has breathing room and space around it.
entries.48:18: The rest of the land alongside the holy area is farmland, and its crops feed the city workers. Ordinary work and food are part of God's plan too.
entries.48:19: People from every tribe of Israel will work this farmland. The city's food comes from the shared labor of all the tribes.
entries.48:20: The whole sacred area, together with the town's land, forms a square. Everything is measured and arranged with precision.
entries.48:21: The land on either side of the holy area and the town belongs to the prince, stretching east and west. The leader is given a place, but the holy things stay at the center.
entries.48:22: The Levites' land and the town's land sit inside the prince's territory, between Judah's and Benjamin's shares. The prince's land surrounds but does not swallow up what is holy.
entries.48:23: The remaining tribes get their shares south of the holy area, starting with Benjamin. The land continues to be divided in an orderly way.
entries.48:24: Simeon's share comes next to Benjamin's, running east to west. Each tribe keeps its own distinct place.
entries.48:25: Issachar's share follows Simeon's, east to west. The pattern of fair portions continues.
entries.48:26: Zebulun's share comes next, east to west. The tribes are arranged in a clear, settled order.
entries.48:27: Gad's share is the last of these southern strips, east to west. Every tribe, even the last listed, has a place.
entries.48:28: Gad's southern border runs from Tamar to the waters near Kadesh and on to the Great Sea. The land has clear boundaries, marking where God's people live.
entries.48:29: This is the land the Lord assigns to Israel's tribes as their inheritance. God himself guarantees the allotment.
entries.48:30: The description now turns to the city's outer edge, starting with the north side and its measurement. The city is laid out with exact dimensions.
entries.48:31: The city gates are named after Israel's tribes, with three gates on the north side. The tribes are honored and included in the city's life.
entries.48:32: The east side also has three gates, named for Joseph, Benjamin, and Dan. Every direction of the city welcomes the tribes.
entries.48:33: The south side has three gates too, named for Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun. The city is open to the tribes from every side.
entries.48:34: The west side has three gates, named for Gad, Asher, and Naphtali. All twelve tribes are represented at the city's entrances.
entries.48:35: The city's total measurement is given, and its name will be 'The Lord is there.' The greatest promise is not the land or the city but God's own presence with his people.
